KAZE VS. MULTIVERSE — REWORKED ACT IV.2 THROUGH ACT VIII.3
Working outline — 2026-10-04

STATUS
User-authorized structural rework. This replaces the old undelivered Act IV Episodes 2–3 plan and earlier assistant-proposed Act V–VIII arrangements. It is not PLAY, not a record that these events occurred, and not a source-package cutover. Delivered Act IV Episode 1 remains intact. Romance OFF.

Entry: afternoon at the cold-store workshop. Chris has a bound forearm wound from Bullseye, with previous injuries retained. A wounded delivery driver arrives with his murdered companion and a toll threat. Kaze closes the book: “Well. Let's go disagree.”

The actual episode did not name Varr or establish his identity to Kaze. Old draft metadata anticipated those details; they are prospective, not actor knowledge. The driver can identify the route and what he witnessed in IV.2. Likewise the gauges' precise interception/custody must be established, not inferred into the delivered scene.

SEASON ENGINE
The main group has stolen money and cargo and wrecked a criminal supply system. Silco tries to recover control; the group's differing priorities make their response dangerous and unpredictable. Their actions disturb the uneasy balance between Zaun, Piltover, scientists, independent killers and outside interests. The central conflict evolves from personal retaliation into a struggle over who can control territory, work, bodies and allegiance.

Silco does not secretly command every subplot. Light judges, 47 fulfills contracts, Jhin composes murders, Punisher pursues his own targets, Hulk seeks his own freedom, Urgot attacks protected authority. Their distinct choices collide with shared people, places and resources.

OUTCOME RULE
The sequence below is the selected planning route, not protected destiny. Actual knowledge, access, speed, power, injury, resources, intent and intervention determine outcomes in prose. Named characters, main characters, audience favorites, future collaborators and scheduled villains receive no survival privilege. Valid regeneration/resistance remains valid; it is not removed to manufacture vulnerability. Neither side is weakened for a longer fight. A missed shot, interrupted killing, retreat or rescue requires a concrete cause. Death persists unless an already-established mechanism genuinely permits something else.

If someone dies sooner, preserve the death and rework the dependent material. Do not arrange a replacement with the same personality/job merely to restore the outline. Planned milestone order remains Vander's death before Silco's death; the staging must respect that order without making either invulnerable. If legitimate intervention prevents an intended milestone, the branch changes rather than overriding the intervention. No on-screen rescue power may be forgotten to force a death.

FUTURE CAST SELECTIONS FOR THIS WORKING OUTLINE
- Punisher: Jon Bernthal portrayal, proposed extraction immediately after The Punisher Season 2 finale. This is the chosen working-plan version, pending source cutover; it is not the existing Earth-616 Punisher (2018) #1 slot. Do not instantiate both automatically. Knowledge remains at the selected screen point; later-pinned Daredevil can remember events earlier Frank does not.
- Savage Hulk: retain the already-selected Earth-616 Incredible Hulk #181-era persona. His Act I appearance was earlier history. Establish his present-day location through the existing original displacement/onset framework and ordinary movement, not a second arrival wave. Do not invent a later shared adventure with Kaze.
- Urgot: working selection is post-Dredge augmentation and subsequent incarceration, consistent with the biography endpoint. Establish this custody on screen before release. His original Dredge escape is not replayed. This resolves the proposed route, not delivered current state or controlling-source activation.
- Sion and Dr. Mundo are not inserted just to complete a matchup list. Sion's later Noxian deployment requires actual authority, transport and access; neither character is needed to repair the present outline. Their wider-season availability is preserved.

ACT IV — THE GROUP STOPS FOLLOWING THE TRAIL

IV.2 — NO MORE TOLLS
Kaze's goal is to remove an obstacle and answer the challenge; Chris wants his purchase and machinery They need not agree about the dead driver's significance.

The toll crew has exploited exchange damage rather than secretly receiving every instruction from Silco. Kaze can stop the demand at its source, with a short decisive fight when the disparity is clear. Recover the identifiable goods and remove the immediate toll operation; the victory does not reveal another indispensable ledger. Chris's wound constrains his work, and he chooses what he can still do rather than becoming helpless. His retrieved equipment has an actual later purpose.

Second consequential thread: Arthur returns to the occupied theatre lead with Daniel. They act on the trap already observed. Jhin's attempt to make Arthur participate in a designed spectacle meets a low-honor gunman willing to destroy the setting and deny the performance. Bring this to a real encounter now. The intended route ends Jhin's immediate theatre operation and can end Jhin himself when Arthur obtains the valid shot. Do not grant a mandatory final monologue or an inevitable escape into the next act. Daniel supplies his own read and action, not just comic accompaniment.

Walt and Jesse accept Silco's initial production arrangement through Singed's already-offered introduction. What appeals to Walt—resources and recognition—comes with control of equipment and output. Jesse sees the work environment and insists on a concrete change, creating their first friction with the employer.

Change that survives: local toll conflict closed; Chris's delivery recovered where evidence supports custody; theatre thread substantially paid off; chemists have an actual patronage relationship. Word of the attacks reaches Silco through survivors or physical evidence. He stops buying more interchangeable bounty crews and begins applying pressure to access, suppliers and relationships.

Viktor thread: continue the established inventor connection through work, with an actual meeting/access route. Viktor identifies a concrete failure in Chris's recovered machinery and helps achieve a limited repair or safer test. Chris retains authorship and practical competence. Show Viktor's dry humor, curiosity and rigorous standards alongside a physical limitation that changes how he works. His illness must not replace his personality or become a repeated cough cue.

Weapon continuity: make Jinx's preparation tangible through servicing Pow-Pow, her rotary gun, and working on the Zapper electrical sidearm. Retain her existing capability and any actual carried damage/ammunition state. Her requested Hextech taser configuration gets an observed power source, test and bounded effect; do not silently conflate every version of Zapper or invent universal paralysis. This preparation answers actual pressure on Silco's operation and is not a detached inventory montage.

THE COUNT occasion 1 — Arthur personally fires one normal-mode fully charged shot during the theatre confrontation. Give him a legitimate line through a load-bearing part of Jhin's prepared firing/trap position and resolve the full penetration, behind-target destruction and structural consequences. Arthur decides whether the line and collateral are acceptable; no automatic hostage-safe geometry or Jhin immunity. The result materially destroys the designed encounter and can kill Jhin if he is actually in the lethal path. Show actual charge time, safety release, ammunition support and aiming opportunity; do not replay the historical first-ever test. Mimir's narration is disrupted in a context-specific way.

IV.3 — SOMEONE ELSE PULLS THE TRIGGER
Dominant collision: Chris pursues Bullseye through the broker already identified in IV.1. He has a personal reason and an actionable connection; there is no new multi-stop clue hunt. Daredevil participates for his own reasons and adjusts after his earlier injuries and defeats. Chris controls his involvement and communicates it; he is not randomly isolated through group incompetence.

Punisher is following that operation's armed personnel through his own observation and evidence. Establish his presence, target and knowledge before his attack. His intervention turns a confrontation into competing attempts to control or kill the same dangerous people. Chris wants agency and a result after being wounded; Daredevil wants to stop the killing; Frank will not promise to leave a murderous target alive for them. Bullseye exploits real angles and openings and remains self-directed.

Preferred twist: Chris's earned actions deny Bullseye an escape/attack, but Punisher takes the lethal shot before Daredevil can secure him. This is not a guaranteed rescue or kill-steal: if Chris, Bullseye, Frank or another present actor wins the causal exchange earlier, retain it. The purpose is a conclusive collision, not a protected rematch booking. The target's survival is not required for Acts V–VIII.

LATEST USER CORRECTION — KAZE / PUNISHER: Kaze is a genuine fan of Jon Bernthal's Punisher and nerds out at encounters. He will not kill Frank, fight back or retaliate even if Frank tries to kill him. Kaze actively protects him against injury, death, capture and other danger using his actual knowledge and available abilities. Defense must not become an attack on Frank. Frank retains independent motives and may reject Kaze's help; fandom does not make him obedient or grant new powers. This supersedes the previous no-admiration/possible-Kaze-kill instruction. Do not fabricate an earlier fan exchange or replay an existing encounter as a first meeting.

Regional decision: Silco abandons the cheap public-bounty approach as his main instrument and contests the relationships that keep Vander influential. Marcus escalates coercive enforcement while calling it order. Trade losses reach Mel and actual foreign commercial contacts; that supplies one route for Noxian attention alongside Ambessa's established family/Hextech interests.

Act end: two local antagonist lanes have real outcomes. The next act begins with a changed enemy strategy, not another financial address. Frank's introduction creates a disagreement about outcomes rather than adding a permanent new team member.

Weapon development: Jayce works at the bench on the Mercury Hammer's combat-ready assembly/refit in response to the escalating threat. The source already authorizes the equipment, so this is visible construction, testing and configuration of the existing design, not an invented claim he never possessed it. A later deliberate decision to deploy it deepens his disagreement with Viktor. Jinx's Pow-Pow becomes a concrete threat in a separate justified intervention or defense; it is not inserted into the Bullseye confrontation merely to add a weapon cameo.

ACT V — THE CITY LOSES ITS BALANCE

V.1 — THE MAN WHO STAYED
Dominant conflict: Silco's economic pressure and Marcus's coercive enforcement converge on Vander's community. Vander makes a consequential decision to stand with people who depend on him rather than legitimize the new arrangement. Vi, Ekko and Jinx have active, different responses to his position; Jinx's divided attachment can no longer remain only a look from Silco's doorway.

The selected route culminates in Vander's death during that conflict, before Silco dies. Establish the concrete geography, hostile action and timing. It cannot rely on an all-powerful rescuer standing nearby and forgetting an available solution. The main group can be occupied by its own causally established decisions; it is not dispatched on an arbitrary errand solely to clear the stage. A valid intervention changes the outcome.

The loss lands differently. Kaze may care about a specific person, resent manipulation or judge the attack through his own interests. Vi and Ekko do not yield ownership of their grief to the main group. Jinx acts because of the loss and conflicting accounts rather than automatically accepting Silco's framing.

Singed's recovery route is shown: who has access to the body, how it is moved, why he obtains it and its condition. No mysterious resurrection cutaway silently fills those gaps. This starts the Warwick research chain; it does not finish it.

Change: the stabilizing figure is gone, community responses become contested action, and Silco inherits instability rather than uncomplicated victory. Walt/Jesse witness or learn the human cost through an actual carrier. Their employer's demands begin changing from a bargain into possession.

Viktor thread: disruption reaches a practical civilian application of his and Jayce's work through real contact or reports. Viktor chooses to spend scarce time/resources on that problem. Jayce faces competing public responsibilities; neither becomes a caricature. Sky participates as a living colleague with her own contribution and judgment, not as a future death announcement.

Weapon payoff: Vi's already-supported Atlas Gauntlets are physically present and used when her position and decisions bring her into the conflict. Show their practical force, limits and cost to the surroundings. Their presence does not make her omnipresent or mandate Vander's rescue/failure. Jinx's tested electrical sidearm offers her a different tactical option from Pow-Pow's sustained fire; its effect depends on the struck target, established mechanism and conditions. Neither weapon waits for a later act when it is already legitimately available.

V.2 — A CLEAN KILL, A DIRTY CITY
Dominant collision: Renata's commercial losses and Marcus's arbitrary seizures give her a concrete independent reason to eliminate him. The working route uses a premium contract reaching 47 through the established brokerage, with actual target verification and planning. No wanted-poster recruitment and no unearned omniscience.

Preferred turn: 47 kills Marcus. It is efficient professional work; the city suffers a complicated result. Marcus's death removes both a corrupt official and a person who knew how his corrupt arrangements functioned. Caitlyn loses a living route to answers, Silco loses leverage, enforcement fragments, and Renata has bought room for her own influence. She has not bought a stable city or ownership of 47.

Urgot is shown in custody before an already-authorized transfer becomes vulnerable amid disrupted command and staffing. His followers and Urgot choose how to exploit the real opportunity. The actual escape unfolds through access and force, not because a missing form magically opens a cell.

Light uses the public crisis as cover and opportunity. Establish his access to public names/faces and the human route used for moving his hidden property if he misses an arranged check-in. That carrier has ordinary access, no special notebook power or understanding. This is the seed for the later empty hiding place, not a new mastermind.

Change: 47's job directly changes the custody/policing situation, which enables Urgot's intervention and complicates Caitlyn's investigation. Ambessa's journey/decision receives actual information through established contacts, with travel and communication time preserved.

Viktor thread: Marcus's death and the resulting institutional disruption delay or restrict an actual research resource. Viktor acts to recover access or redesign the work, and challenges Jayce over a specific decision. The emerging disagreement is about who benefits from progress and how long suffering people are expected to wait. Illness sharpens his urgency without making disability the cause of moral corruption.

V.3 — WHO GETS TO BE STRONG
Dominant conflict: Urgot converts freedom into an attack on protected local authority. He is not Silco's lieutenant. His ideology becomes visible through whom he threatens, what he demands and what his followers do.

Urgot interprets protection as interference with his test of strength. This gives the fight a point without making Kaze the moral center. If the power gap ends it quickly, end it; no secret durability upgrade, withheld transformation or hostage freeze exists merely to prolong him.

The intended episode resolves the immediate Urgot confrontation. Death, disabling or a legitimately caused escape is preserved, not selected to guarantee another round. Followers retain individual motives rather than vanishing as one hive mind when their leader falls.

The local violence and changed access displace people and activity into the industrial outskirts. Establish credible reports of a huge green being there, then a present-day audience observation of Savage Hulk, already displaced through the original onset framework. This supplies location and context for the next act without a new cosmic arrival.

Act end: Vander is lost, Marcus's selected death has institutional fallout, and an anti-ruler movement has forced another factional response. The pressure has reached a living Hulk; it has not summoned him as a finale monster.

Weapon development: Caitlyn's experience against increasingly dangerous opponents motivates a specific Hextech rifle commission through actual workshop contact. Jayce contributes engineering; Caitlyn supplies requirements and evaluates handling/accuracy. Existing firearm skill transfers without granting instant mastery of every new operating characteristic. Viktor challenges a concrete design priority or diversion of resources while retaining his independent work. Establish materials, component custody and elapsed build time; no automatic gift appears between scenes.

THE COUNT occasion 2 — establish Arthur's reason, notice and physical route into the wider Urgot conflict before he acts. Arthur personally fires a second normal-mode fully charged shot against a legitimately established hostile position, obstructing emplacement or Urgot himself if the available line and intent support it. It changes the engagement or accessible terrain. No durability buff saves a struck opponent, and no required miss preserves Urgot f. Their meaningful action can occur before or alongside Arthur's independent shot; nobody pauses a valid lethal action to allocate credit. Preserve directional damage beyond the initial impact.

ACT VI — POWER CANNOT SOLVE EVERY KIND OF CONTROL

VI.1 — LEAVE HULK ALONE
Dominant collision: show what Savage Hulk wants in his present situation. Local armed actors interfering with him create a concrete conflict; the episode establishes their motive and access rather than assuming anyone can capture him.

Kaze recognizes the earlier encounter within what was actually established. His appetite for meaningful intensity can conflict with Hulk's wish to be left alone. Curiosity can make Kaze listen, test a boundary or choose a fight; recognition does not guarantee friendship. Hulk chooses his own response. A confrontation uses the pinned Savage persona and real Kaze toolkit, with no imported Worldbreaker/TOBA feats and no compulsory draw or mutual admiration.

They do not automatically become a Hulk-restraint squad. If Kaze provokes damage, keep him responsible rather than assigning all blame to Hulk.

Physical destruction or changes in access affect the already-pressured production sites and routes. Silco responds by demanding relocation and tighter control over the chemists and labor. Information about the encounter reaches the political actors through witnesses and material damage; their decisions use what they can reasonably know.

Change: the Act I callback alters the current conflict. Hulk's choice at the end—departure, continued resistance or another earned outcome—matters. He is not a free serum ingredient, commanded siege weapon or guaranteed survivor.

Viktor thread: consequences of the Hulk encounter change a previously established scientific or civilian need. Viktor's intervention provides a useful but bounded result and consumes time or material he needed elsewhere. Dominant action: Walter and Jesse break with Silco. The motive groundwork from IV.2 and Act V now pays off. Jesse refuses the human cost; Walt refuses subordination and loss of control over his work. These reasons overlap without making them morally equivalent.

Silco's relocation order creates a moving, active confrontation instead of a lab-paper raid. Chris contributes an actual engineering solution using tools salvaged and examined earlier. Chris becomes the active owner of his enhancement project, with Walt and Jesse contributing their bounded expertise. He does not become Walt's passive test subject. Walt's impulse to take credit/control can create immediate friction without turning the alliance into a predetermined betrayal.

Kaze's voluntary single blood sample bargains for ongoing Singed collaboration. Singed remains autonomous and retains his own research and daughter motive; this is not his defection or a purchase of his allegiance. The blood is payment, not an automatically approved serum ingredient.

Parallel decision with a definite consequence: before detention, Light schedules the bounded bathhouse death and has already established his ordinary missed-check-in property-movement arrangement. Change: the chemists' role and patronage genuinely change. The serum becomes an active collaboration with real sourcing gaps; it does not become finished chemistry by montage. Singed now has competing work interests; no secret automatic sharing of one project's discoveries with another.

Viktor thread: Chris's new collaboration creates a plausible scientific contact through their existing inventor relationship. Viktor sees a specific observed result or voluntarily shared finding, not the entire serum plan. His personal urgency gives him a reason to reopen his own contact with Singed. Viktor seeks answers independently; Walt, Jesse and Chris do not automatically gain access to his private work. Singed's willingness to help never establishes trustworthiness.

THE COUNT occasion 3 — during the chemists' escape, Arthur personally uses a normal-mode fully charged shot to defeat an established physical barrier or pursuit position when it materially enables their chosen route. VI.3 — THE DEATH THAT WAS ALREADY ORDERED
Dominant confrontation: Caitlyn's evidence leads to Light's detention. Kaze's curiosity and intolerance of evasive answers drive a focused interrogation using legitimately available channels. No unused obvious solution is ignored to keep Light mysterious for another act. Seeing Ryuk is not automatically hearing him; ordinary Caitlyn/Vi perception requires actual fragment contact. Ryuk is autonomous, not an exposition service.

Resolve Light's personal confrontation here when the actual encounter permits it. Kaze may kill, restrain, exploit or release him according to supported intent and mechanics. A plan for later notebook consequences does not preserve Light's body. An issued valid death instruction and a physically moved object can outlast their author.

Act end: three established pressures have substantial payoffs—Hulk's return, the chemists' break and Kira's confrontation. None is merely promised again.

Weapon payoff: Caitlyn now has the Hextech rifle if the preceding build and tests succeeded. Establish its performance through a justified field use, not by forcing her to shoot during Light's interrogation. It changes her practical options without identifying hidden guilt, cancelling notebook mechanics, or guaranteeing a hit. Jayce's own hammer deployment and consequences must similarly be shown when his actual responsibilities bring him into danger, with ownership of the decision remaining his.

ACT VII — THE PAST COMES BACK WRONG

USER-DIRECTED VIKTOR AND SERUM PROGRESSION — 2026-10-04
Newest explicit user correction controls the remaining outline: Viktor's existing illness must become an urgent health crisis; he experiments with Shimmer and Hextech/Hexcore; that experiment kills Sky; Viktor then begins his transformation. Slow burn now has a definite progression across VII.1–3. Each appearance must advance the health crisis, dangerous intervention, fatal consequence or visible transformation. ACTIVE PRESENTATION CORRECTION — 2026-10-04
User found the delivered VI.3 fight confusing because environmental mechanisms displaced the people fighting. This is a forward correction to VII–VIII, not a replay or erasure of VI.3. The outline below remains prospective: no future encounter, death, choice, form or new research result is delivered/accepted by this edit.

Fight clarity: name who is attacking whom and what each wants before complicating the exchange. Give the listener a few simple positions, then narrate attack -> response -> visible consequence. Stay with one confrontation until a meaningful beat resolves; an intercut must earn its interruption, and the return names the people and immediate danger again. Do not make listeners reconstruct simultaneous portal, winch, chain, wagon and pressure-vessel mechanics. Environmental damage can be huge and consequential; describe its immediate effect simply, then return to the combatants. A signature attack must be understandable from its action and result without a terminology lecture.

Dramatic force: build anticipation before a major clash, let recognizable participants pursue incompatible personal goals, and leave room for the impact or revelation to register. Resolve clearly outmatched opponents decisively. Tension may come from a valued relationship, a threatened objective, a choice or genuinely unknown capability; never suppress earned perception/powers or invent equality. The main group initiates and confronts as well as reacts. No replacement pattern of anonymous attackers arriving to damage equipment while the group handles another industrial accident.

Character presence: Kaze chooses through his actual curiosity, attachment, appetite, pride and impatience; he is not restricted to irritated jokes and convenient rescue. His eyes, body and other earned systems change exchanges when useful. Daniel has perception, strategy, mobility and independent choices Chris's actual RDR2, kitchen language, looting, engineering and Teemo friction affect choices instead of becoming obligatory cutaways. Billy owns his decisions and exterior time. Arthur has individual brutality and tactical competence between Count uses. Their different priorities may collide without instant consensus or a mandatory argument in every scene.

Emotional rhythm and voice: distinguish suspense, violent release, shock, grief and absurd comedy. Do not puncture every serious beat with a quip or use a single flat cadence of short fragments throughout. Black Mimir gives brief useful orientation, personality and genuine reactions; he does not explain the writing rules. Brutal bodily consequences stay visible where the fight earns them, with injuries and regeneration narrated distinctly. More gore alone is not a substitute for a memorable confrontation.

Subplot movement: choose the threads whose decisions alter this episode's conflict. Let the consequence reach the next actor through an actual contact, witness or event, then change that actor's choice. No courtesy tour of every subplot, repeated custody paperwork, generic laboratory repair sequence or end-of-episode status roll call. Preserve needed time for recovery, but advance Viktor through the user-directed illness -> Shimmer/Hexcore experiment -> Sky's death -> beginning transformation sequence across Act VII. Choices and disagreements carry that development; they cannot replace its payoffs.

NARRATION FLOW — LATEST USER CORRECTION
User finds the entire narration choppy and disconnected. Use connected paragraphs, varied sentence lengths, clear referents and natural causal transitions. Reserve isolated fragments for selected impacts rather than every movement and line of thought. Finish a meaningful exchange before cutting away, and briefly orient the listener upon return. Mimir remains the sole narrator with personality and emotional range; smooth narration is not a neutral summary voice. No TTS speed change is implied.

AGENT 47 CONTINUITY AND RE-ENTRY
Last delivered operation is the V.2 Marcus assassination for Renata through a premium intermediary; 47 leaves by the service exit, and Renata receives confirmation. Exact current location/next contract remain unknown. His active thread must re-enter the remaining acts through a consequential independent operation with a real client/objective, information, preparation and access. Do not invent an already-running secret job or replay Marcus's killing. A new contract affecting the succession/ownership conflict is an implementation option, not an assigned target or delivered event. Establish the next operation early enough for its actions to alter another character's choices; do not save him for an unexplained finale cameo. Preserve mature post-HITMAN-3/Freelancer World of Assassination fidelity, equipment limits and lack of omniscience. His methods may use the environment when the setup/result is immediately understandable.

VII.1 — VANDER'S VOICE
Dominant collision: Singed's work produces an active Warwick only after the preceding recovery and meaningful research time. Allow lived days/weeks where needed across acts; energetic narration is not proof all events happen within two afternoons.

No automatic new assimilation reward is awarded.

Chris / Walter / Jesse payoff: demonstrate the first useful Shimmer-derived research component rather than report another repair. Walter makes the separation/process work; Jesse runs the taught method himself and reproduces the result, giving him an indispensable contribution beyond reacting to Walter. Chris observes a plainly understandable comparison and decides what the result permits in his project. Show the actual material access, experiment and outcome; do not invent a finished test history inside the seventeen-day montage. Singed's existing contribution supplies relevant biology, not universal expertise or access to the missing Extremis/ocular branches.

The result gives Walter something valuable to control, Jesse a reason to defend a genuinely constructive use of his skills, and Chris a concrete advance toward his enhancement. Viktor thread — VII.1, health crisis and the decision: his existing illness worsens enough to interrupt his work and force an immediate decision about survival. Vander/Warwick matters to this decision as an observed example of Singed sustaining and altering living function; Viktor does not acquire a cure or a whole transformation system by looking at him. VII.2 — WHAT SILCO WON'T SELL
Dominant conflict: a real opportunity for a political or operational settlement demands a concession involving Jinx. State that demand and its human cost plainly. The central confrontation is personal: what Jinx now believes about Vander, what Silco actually did or concealed, and what each will choose when confronted. Use only discoveries the branch has genuinely supplied, not imported private knowledge. Bring the people concerned face to face through actual access. ACT VI — EPISODE 3
THE DEATH THAT WAS ALREADY ORDERED

The first bullet came through Kaze’s shortcut and blew the back off Caitlyn’s empty chair.

She dropped beside the desk.

Vi turned toward the hole in the wall.

On the other side, in a workshop across the district, Chris shouted, “BEHIND!”

Something heavy struck flesh. A man screamed.

Kaze looked through the opening.

“Oh, now something happens.”

At a quarter to six, Caitlyn had collected Light Yagami from his lodging house. Osric Pell, the bathhouse owner who rented rooms to Silco’s wage collectors, had identified him: the polite stranger who borrowed Caitlyn’s authority to obtain a man’s full name and portrait. That man was now dead.

Light had left with Vi on one side and Caitlyn on the other.

“Keep our usual arrangements,” he’d told Mera, his landlady.

At six, she paid the waiting porter to move his locked case. Instructions given days before. An ordinary errand continuing while its owner answered questions somewhere else.

Kaze had joined the interview because a man who might kill without touching you sounded worth meeting. Daniel came too, bottle in hand, bare feet on Caitlyn’s windowsill.

They arrived through a portal from Renata’s workshop.

Kaze left it open.

Caitlyn sent an officer to collect Pell for their arranged morning conversation. Kaze sat backward on a chair and expected to get bored quickly.

Which explains how an interview acquired a fucking loading bay.

Light sat motionless through the gunshot. His eyes went to the wall clock.

Six eighteen.

At the workshop, Jesse Pinkman had a rifle under his chin.

The man holding it belonged to Silco’s recovery crew. Six men, a loading wagon, a powered winch. They’d watched Kaze and Daniel leave and decided the remaining strangers would care enough about the chemists to negotiate.

The chemists were their leverage; the machinery was their target. Silco’s instructions were collection first. Break whatever couldn’t be taken.

Their foreman had started with the second part.

His bullet shattered Chris’s new pressure controls. The winch was already pulling on the laboratory frame. A pipe tore loose, spraying hot coolant across the floor.

Inside Catfish Billy, Chris’s controller hit the couch.

Red Dead Redemption Two paused with Arthur Morgan halfway through stealing a wagon.

“Some fucking professionalism,” Chris said. “That’s all I ask.”

Billy stood beside the workshop entrance, watching Jesse’s captor back toward the loading cart.

“Release him,” Billy said pleasantly. “You’re obstructing my breakfast.”

“Billy. Let me out.”

The catfish’s broad mouth opened. Split wider. Flesh rolled inward in wet folds as Chris pushed through, boots landing in the same bloody space Billy had occupied. The great belly and shoulders turned inside out around him.

The gunman stared.

Arthur came through the yard door at his back.

His metal hand closed over the rifle and wrenched its muzzle away from Jesse. The gunman fired. That was the shot through the portal.

Arthur drove his other forearm through the man’s elbow.

Bone broke through the sleeve.

Jesse ducked as Arthur dragged the ruined arm across the man’s throat, turned him toward the empty loading yard and fired UNSHAKEN into his ribs.

The exit wound painted the wagon boards.

“Behind!” Chris shouted.

The foreman swung his pistol toward Arthur.

Chris’s left hand was already drawing HAMMER TIME. His injured right wrist stayed tucked against his chest. For one cold instant, the turn of the pistol, the foreman’s exposed shoulder and the second rifleman beyond him separated into clean, useful decisions.

Dead Eye.

Two shots.

The foreman’s shoulder burst backward. The rifleman hit the doorframe without the upper part of his jaw.

“Two orders up.”

“Your kitchen’s on fire,” Teemo said.

“No shit, you haunted fucking crouton.”

A third man had tipped a burning bottle into the packing material behind the apparatus. Flame climbed the oily wrapping. He ran for the alley.

Kaze stepped through the portal.

His right red eye caught Arthur’s turn: elbow trapped, shoulder checked, the opponent’s own backward pull used to expose his neck.

Kaze smiled.

The fleeing man collided with him.

Kaze copied the turn. Same hook, same shoulder placement. His living black forearm lengthened to keep the hold as the man tried to wrench free.

Then Kaze’s other hand passed across the exposed throat.

BLACKCURRENT made no sound.

The head struck the floor. The body took another step into the wall.

“Nice,” Kaze said to Arthur.

Arthur glanced at him over his revolver.

“Yours made a mess.”

“So did yours.”

“Ain’t a complaint.”

Through the opening behind them, Light moved his watch beneath the table.

His thumb found the concealed catch. A writing point slid toward the scrap of paper inside.

Daniel saw it.

A bare foot hooked Light’s wrist and turned it upward. Before the point could make a useful stroke, Kaze looked back through the portal.

Light made the mistake of meeting the red eye.

His fingers stopped.

His whole body refused him.

Daniel took the watch.

“Bad time to write a complaint.”

At the workshop, the winch operator opened the throttle.

The chain snapped taut. The apparatus lurched toward the door, dragging a bolted bench across the floor. Walter grabbed the sample rack. Jesse grabbed the young fitter pinned between that bench and the wall.

The lad had come with the escaped workers. He’d spent the night making this place useful.

Now a broken bracket had opened his thigh.

“Help me!” Jesse shouted.

Walter looked from the rack to the blood spreading under the bench.

“Walt!”

He put the rack down.

Together they heaved. The bench shifted barely an inch.


“Get him out.”

Jesse dragged the fitter backward. Walter pressed a folded apron against the wound.


Then up at the man.

“Really?”

Wood burst inward. The gunman folded around the blow, blood coming out between his teeth.


The rifle fired once under the falling body.

Nobody fired it again.

The winch kept pulling.

Its operator had abandoned the controls and jumped. The wagon slewed across the threshold. One wheel mounted a broken slab; the tall loaded frame began tipping toward Jesse and the injured fitter.


His body swelled. Paws ground into the yard as his shoulders climbed to eight feet, white markings standing against green fur, eyes paling beneath a rush of gold light.

Gamma Super Saiyan.

He barked once at the people in his path.

They moved.


The air dented around it. Iron crumpled between teeth that were nowhere near the iron. His projected bite held; his enormous body took the load.

He dug in and wrenched his head sideways.

The wagon flipped away from Jesse.

Its fleeing operator vanished beneath it.

There was one scream, cut short by the sound of the axle hitting stone. Blood spread beneath the bed.


Good lad. The delivery’s been fucking declined.

Inside, the damaged pressure vessel began to shriek.

Walter reached for the shutoff.

“Power’s already off!” Chris yelled. “It’s still under pressure!”

He pointed toward the broken controls.

“Vent’s jammed. That seam opens, we’re eating the fucking boiler.”

Kaze looked at the vessel.

A second opening spread beneath the apparatus.

The ruined frame dropped through it into the empty yard, well away from the overturned wagon and the people at the entrance. Kaze closed the workshop end, stepped outside and opened his hand.

Black fire took the burning packing material still clinging to the frame. He extinguished that flame as soon as the fuel was consumed.

The pressure remained.

“Back,” Chris said.

Everyone else was inside, away from the doorway.

Kaze stood alone in the yard. BLACKCURRENT extended from his hand in a thin spear and sliced the damaged vessel from five metres away.

The seam opened.

Steam hammered the paving. Torn metal hit the opposite brick wall. A thick plate buried itself where the wagon had stood seconds before. Another piece took Kaze’s hand off.

He glanced at the spraying stump. Black cords lashed out, caught the falling hand and drew it back against his wrist. The fingers flexed as the last strands knitted.

“Hot,” he said.

The yard rang.

Arthur looked around the edge of the doorway.

Chris stared at the scattered remains of his controls.

“Three days.”

Kaze looked back.

“What?”

“Three fucking days of work.”

“You want me to put the explosion back?”

In the interview room, Caitlyn touched the paper Daniel had laid on the desk.

A towering creature appeared above Light’s shoulder: long limbs, jagged grin, eyes bright with delight at other people’s disasters.

She recoiled.

Vi raised a gauntlet toward apparently empty air.

“What?”

Caitlyn held out the scrap.

“Touch it.”

Vi did.

“Oh, fuck off.”

Ryuk laughed.

Kaze returned from the workshop and looked up at him. His purple left eye had seen the death god all morning. The moving mouth still supplied no sound.

He touched the paper.

Ryuk’s laughter arrived halfway through a wheeze.

“That’s better,” Kaze said.

Daniel touched it too.

“That’s debatable.”

Vi secured Light’s wrists and searched him. Caitlyn took the writing point and watch. Daniel stayed between the prisoner and the fragment.

Kaze released the paralysis.

Light gasped. The clock clicked over.

Six twenty.

Across the district, Osric Pell finished checking the steam-room latch.

His heart stopped.

He struck the bench on the way down. By the time the cleaner and Caitlyn’s waiting officer forced the door, his face was against the wet tiles.

The officer turned him over. Started compressions.

In the interview room, Light’s shoulders eased by a fraction.

Kaze saw it.

All that blood through the doorway, all that loss of control—and now relief.

“What did you just get?”

Light looked at him.

“You’ve been enjoying yourself.”

“I asked you something.”

“And I’ve asked what crime you think I’ve committed.”

Kaze came closer. Black tissue still moved along his right arm. A bead of someone else’s blood ran over his knuckles.

Light’s eyes caught on it.

There. Beneath the composure. The fear of being exposed, stripped of the thing that made every other person in the room a possible victim. The fear of dying as an ordinary man while someone else held his secret.

Kaze took hold of that fear.

Light saw the notebook open across Caitlyn’s desk.

It wasn’t there.

Every name he dreaded seeing discovered appeared beneath her hand. His own voice began reading them. His own careful handwriting spread across the walls.

He tried to look away.

The room turned with him.

Kaze found the secrets fastened to that terror: a name, a face held in mind, death given instructions. The bathhouse entry. Last night. Six twenty. The locked case in Mera’s storage alcove.

The false pages vanished.

Light was breathing through his teeth.

“Get out.”

Kaze looked at Caitlyn.

“He wrote Pell’s death last night. Six twenty. Book’s in a locked case at his lodging house.”

Her gaze flicked to the clock.

“You know that how?”

“It’s what he’s terrified you’ll find.”

Caitlyn turned to the door and called for another officer to go to the bathhouse. Then she faced Light again.

“A name and a photograph,” she said. “That’s why you wanted both.”

Light held her gaze.

What Kaze had pulled from him was no signed confession. No witness had yet put the notebook in her hands.

But Caitlyn had stopped looking at the little scrap as though it were merely paper.

At the workshop, the wounded foreman tried to crawl beneath a cabinet.

Chris caught him by the belt and hauled him back out.

“Who sent you?”

“You know who.”

“Then why the fuck did you come?”

The man looked toward the wrecked yard.

“They said the dangerous ones had left.”

Chris turned toward Arthur.

“You hearing this disrespect?”

Arthur lit his cigar from a surviving curl of flame.

“Heard worse.”

The foreman’s good hand disappeared under his coat.

“Knife,” Teemo snapped.

Chris shifted away from the reach. Billy forced the change before he could answer: jaw unfolding, flesh swallowing flesh, Chris disappearing inward as the catfish’s bulk rolled into the room.

Billy caught the knife wrist.

Pulled the man against his belly.

Opened his mouth.

The foreman saw the rows of serrated teeth and tried to brace both feet against the floor.

Billy bit down through his shoulder and chest.

The scream became a wet choking sound. One heel hammered twice against the cabinet. Then the legs went slack.

Billy swallowed the dead man in two ugly contractions.

“Dangerous is such an unhelpful word,” he said. “Before breakfast.”

Inside, Chris stood in the boys’ club, splashed with somebody else’s blood.

His game remained paused.

“You could have asked,” he said.

“You were being stabbed.”

“I’d moved.”

“And I was hungry. We both had a morning.”

At the station, the officer returned with wet knees and blood on his cuff from Pell’s split scalp.

“Dead.”

Light looked directly at Caitlyn.

“I’ve been here the entire time.”

“Yes,” she said. “While a death arranged last night happened this morning.”

His expression changed.

No indignation now. Calculation searching for its next surface.

“The superintendent was corrupt. Pell helped collectors bleed people who couldn’t afford to eat. You know what this city rewards.”

Vi leaned against the door.

“So you’re doing us a favour.”

“I can remove people you can’t touch.”

“And eventually,” Caitlyn said, “people who disagree with you.”

Light turned to Kaze.

“You understand. You just killed men without asking a court.”

“Yes.”

“You don’t object to killing.”

“No.”

“You object to someone else choosing.”

Kaze smiled.

“Now you’re listening.”

Caitlyn stepped forward.

“He’s secured. We’re taking him into custody.”

Light looked from her to Kaze and understood, too late, that finding a man’s hypocrisy was useful only if the man needed to deny it.

“The notebook can—”

Black tissue hardened along Kaze’s hand.

Caitlyn moved across his path.

“Don’t.”

His forearm bent around her without a joint.

The blade entered beneath Light’s jaw. Passed through the roof of his mouth and into his brain.

The chair jerked against the floor.

Vi seized Kaze’s forearm. Her gauntlet crushed it with a sound like a boot grinding wet gravel.

Blood ran down Light’s throat, soaked his collar and dripped between his bound wrists.

He did not finish the sentence.

Kaze looked at Vi’s grip. Black strands drew the ruined arm back together between the metal fingers.

“Let go.”

“You first.”

He withdrew the blade. Light sagged against the restraints.

“Vi,” Caitlyn said.

She opened the gauntlet.

For a moment nobody spoke.

Ryuk watched the body. Still smiling, though the laughter had stopped.

“He tried to use the paper,” Kaze said.

“And you stopped him,” Caitlyn answered. “Then you killed my prisoner.”

Kaze glanced toward the desk.

“You know where the book is.”

“I also know what happens when I invite you into an interview. Leave.”

He stood still.

“You don’t touch my evidence. You don’t question my prisoners. You don’t get my cooperation because you’ve found something interesting.”

Daniel remained beside the desk.

“I’ll help find the case.”

Kaze looked at him.

Daniel drank from his bottle and waited.

No apology. No request for permission.

“All right,” Kaze said.

He went through the portal and closed it behind him.

Back in the workshop, Billy allowed Chris out to examine the wreckage.

Chris immediately crouched beside the fallen rifleman and began unbuckling a tool pouch.

Kaze stared.

“The floor’s still hot.”

“So is the loot.”


“Nice watch.”

“Don’t,” Kaze said.


“He thinks you’ll miss it.”

Chris took the watch.

Kaze kicked the empty pouch across the room.


Then Jesse appeared in the doorway, supporting the fitter. Walter had tied the pressure dressing in place; blood was already reaching the outer cloth.

“We need a clinic. Now.”

Jesse ran ahead to find a clinic.


The laughter stopped while they carried the lad out.

The clinic saved the leg. Walking on it would be another matter for a while.

The equipment wasn’t getting up at all.

Mera’s storage shelf was empty when Caitlyn arrived.

“He missed his collection,” the landlady said. “I did what he paid me to do.”

She gave them the porter’s name, Marlo, and the address on the delivery instruction. He circled, snorted and returned .

So they used the bloody address.

Marlo, a day porter eating breakfast at Channer Yard, remembered a light case and a generous fee. He took them to the rented storeroom and complained about his cooling eggs.

Daniel opened the ordinary lock with a touch and a murmured syllable.

Caitlyn lifted the lid.

The notebook was there.

Pell’s name. The superintendent’s. Others that would have to be connected to actual people.

A weapon small enough to carry under an arm. A city had been bleeding around it while its owner smiled at breakfast.

Caitlyn closed it. The book, watch and fragment went into restricted evidence storage under her custody.

Nobody wrote a test name.

That evening, Kaze asked Daniel what else they’d found.

“Ask Caitlyn.”

“She told me to fuck off.”

“I was there.”

Kaze watched his friend take a drink.

Then nodded.

“Fair.”

Inside Billy, Chris finally resumed his game. On the other monitor, the catfish’s hat feed showed a slow walk through Zaun. The bell rang above the boys’ club doorway. Charles, the great mechanical fish sign, hung near the Piltover wayfinding sign Chris had no sensible reason to own.

Teemo watched Arthur Morgan kneel beside a body.

“You’re doing it again.”

“This one didn’t shoot my pressure regulator.”

“Low standards.”

“Shut the fuck up. I’m relaxing.”

A scrape came from MEAT CANYON.

One of the two captured exchange guards had used a loose fitting to work his restraint far enough aside to stand. He took a step, looked up at the living ceiling and stopped.

Billy’s voice rolled through the chamber.

“Wonderful. Now you can stretch before making another poor decision.”

Chris paused, listened, then went back to the game.

Outside, Billy chose his own street.

The next seventeen days cost money, sleep and skin.

Renata’s people arrived to find her workshop sprayed with blood and her new tenants sweeping up pieces of the apparatus they’d negotiated to use. She kept the floor available. She charged for the damage.

Chris pinned the bill above the replacement bench.

Walter took it down.

Chris nailed it back up.

Jesse changed the loading arrangement so an entire room could no longer be dragged behind one machine. Arthur helped move the surviving frame. Later his body shrank out of gamma, back to his usual formidable size. He spent two afternoons refusing to leave the fitter’s crutch alone.

Chris’s wrist stayed strapped. His rebuilt controls failed once, loudly. Nobody stood beside them for the next test.

The serum remained unfinished. Cleverness hadn’t conjured its missing ingredients. What they had now was equipment they understood better and a much less polite working relationship.

Silco’s production slowed without his chemists. His recovery crew did not return. Renata kept the workshop open anyway.

And Viktor kept visiting Singed.

He watched preserved muscle in Vander’s dead arm contract under stimulation.

“That moved,” Singed said.

“Vander did not,” Viktor answered.

Yet he returned. Asked different questions. Stayed longer.

At his own bench, Sky helped him build a small runic test frame for an organic sample. A green shoot straightened when they powered the field.

She disconnected it.

The shoot folded.

Viktor’s hand went to the switch.

“Wait,” Sky said. “We need to see what it does without us.”

He stopped.

They watched until the measurement was complete.

Then he restored the power.

Sky left at the end of the evening. Viktor stayed. His leg ached beneath the bench. A cough left a red spot on the cloth he folded and put away.

Inside the vessel, the little shoot stood upright.

The building lights went out one floor at a time.

Viktor reached down and plugged his apparatus into the overnight supply.

ACT VI — EPISODE 2
WE ARE NOT YOUR PROPERTY

Jesse wanted the workers out.

Walter wanted the apparatus, his retained samples and the right to decide what happened to his own work.

Chris wanted both men at a bench where nobody could order him to drink the result.

Aye. Three men can agree to leave a burning house while arguing bitterly about which part belongs to them.

They met twice during the relocation. Jesse came with the wagons returning for equipment. Walter came the second time, ostensibly to reject a faulty pressure assembly Chris had been asked to examine.

Kaze listened until Walt used the phrase “proprietary considerations.”

“Say ownership.”

Walter stopped.

“What?”

“It's shorter. You're worried about ownership.”

“I'm concerned that the people involved understand the value of—”

“There he goes again,” Daniel said from under the workbench.

Chris folded his arms.

“It's my enhancement project. You help with chemistry. Jesse helps with process and practical work. Neither of you gets to put anything in me because you like a graph.”

“Enhancement from what?” Walter asked.

Chris gave him the broad design: an integrated treatment, several biological components still missing, a need to separate useful Shimmer effects from the damage, and a long road before anything belonged in a human body.

Walter asked three precise questions.

Chris answered two and told him the third had no honest answer yet.

That interested Walt more than a promise would have.

“You need someone who understands control.”

“I need someone who can work without becoming Dutch with a fucking lab coat.”

Jesse looked at him.

“Who?”

“Guy with a plan. Everybody else pays for it.”

Walter's mouth tightened.

Daniel laughed underneath the bench.

Good. They understood each other just enough to begin a dangerous working relationship.

Across the river, Caitlyn stood in an empty quarry with Jayce beside her and the first Hextech rifle assembly braced on a testing rest.

It had taken three working days to reach this point. The first mount had shifted under recoil. The second had scorched its own insulation. Jayce had rebuilt the coupling while Caitlyn mapped where every failed shot landed.

Now the powered round punched through the angled test plate and buried itself in the cleared earth beyond.

Caitlyn checked the bore, the coupling and the plate before she smiled.

“Again.”

Jayce handed her the next load.

Viktor had helped examine the stresses, but he wasn't here. Sky had made him keep the appointment to rebuild his support mechanism. For once, the world's problems had been obliged to survive two hours without him.

By the final test, Caitlyn could put the rifle's additional force where she intended and shut the powered system down cleanly afterward. Jayce put a hand on the stock before she packed it away.

“If the coupling shifts, stop.”

“I watched what it did when it shifted.”

He nodded.

That was better than a promise made by somebody who'd missed the explosion.

At the ore station, the relocation had acquired locks.

The man supervising them was Hask, one of Silco's production overseers. He controlled the keys, the guards and the loading schedule. He had put the workers' families in a goods carriage while the last machinery came uphill.

“Temporary accommodation,” he told Jesse.

Jesse looked through the barred ventilation opening at a woman trying to settle two frightened children.

“It's a fucking box.”

“They're together.”

“Then get in with them.”

Hask struck him across the face with the key ring.

Jesse stumbled against the carriage.

“Remember what you're paid for.”

Walter saw it from the loading platform. He looked at the two guards beside Hask, then at the remaining laboratory cases.

“We are leaving,” he told Jesse when Hask moved away.

Jesse wiped his mouth.

“Yeah. We are.”

He pointed toward the carriage.

Walt looked at it. Then he nodded once.

Chris arrived with the final machinery wagon. Arthur drove.

Kaze and Daniel had entered through the same yard during the previous day's inspection. Now Kaze stood in the empty workshop Renata's buyer had made available, fixing its space in his attention before opening a passage back to the loading platform he had actually seen.

Renata had received three promised equipment repairs in exchange for temporary use of the floor. Chris had struck out her claim to future inventions before agreeing.

Daniel had made him read that sentence twice.

Miracles do occur. Occasionally they involve literacy under protest.

Chris climbed off the wagon and glanced at the goods carriage.

“That's not on the packing list.”

“Keep working,” Hask said.

Teemo's voice went quiet.

“Two above you. One at the rear door.”

“Saw them.”

“Then stop looking at the fucking winch.”

“I'm looking at the brake.”

Chris knelt beside it with the hand tool he'd taken after Urgot's death. Hask had locked the carriage brake so the workers couldn't roll it downhill. The release linkage was exposed beneath the housing.

Chris fitted the tool and began backing it off.

Above them, a rifleman noticed Jesse passing a laboratory case through a black opening that hadn't been in the wall a moment earlier.

He raised his weapon.

Arthur shot him before he found the trigger.

The report struck the yard. Hask reached for his pistol. Walter drove the heavy lid of a packing case into his wrist, breaking his grip, and Jesse hit him with the case itself.

Hask fell off the platform.

“Service!” Chris shouted.

The guard at the carriage door turned his rifle on him.

A shot from beyond the fence hit the guard under the jaw.

Frank Castle stepped out of the narrow gap between two storage sheds. He'd followed the families here, watched the locking routine and waited until he had a clear line on the armed men keeping them inside.

Now he crossed to the carriage.

“Away from the door.”

He waited until the faces withdrew before shooting the exposed lock.

Frank opened the door and stood aside.

“Stay low. Keep moving.”

He didn't introduce himself. The skull on his vest was doing quite enough talking.

On the platform, a second rifleman charged Kaze with a fixed bayonet.

Kaze caught the barrel, planted his foot against the rail and folded beneath the thrust. The late turn he'd taken from Daniel at the smelter brought him around the man's guard.

This time there was no mountain of green muscle at the other end.

The rifleman hit the deck face-first. Kaze broke his neck with one short movement and kicked the rifle toward the wall.

“People first,” he told Jesse. “Then your boxes.”

Walter reached for the nearest case anyway.

Kaze looked at him.

Walter moved aside.

Chris freed the carriage brake and used the salvaged pump to lift the jammed linkage clear. He pressed his broad side along the exposed edge, making a moving wall between them and the last firing position.

He snarled, turned toward the muzzle flash and barked.

The focused pressure caught the rifleman behind his low barricade. Wood burst. The man tumbled backward out of sight.


There. A dog the size of a delivery wagon, still waiting half a heartbeat to make certain his person was coming.

Chris drew CHOW MAIN with his injured hand, found the grip unreliable and changed weapons instead of pretending the wrist had healed for the occasion. HAMMER TIME came up in his left.

For a breath the yard separated into moving pieces: an exposed elbow, a rifle swinging across the families' path, the instant before a man fired.

Dead Eye gave him the opening. He used it.

The rifleman dropped.

“Eighty-six the asshole on the stairs.”

Teemo growled, “Reload.”

“Yes, chef.”

“Don't call me—”

“Then stop running my fucking station.”

Chris reloaded.

Hask crawled behind a moving ore cart and reached the signal rope leading to the far loading gate. He yanked it hard.

Beyond the yard, a powered gun carriage rolled into position at the head of the old ore cutting. Its crew had been guarding the incoming stock. Now they turned the weapon toward the platform.

Arthur saw its armored front swing into line.

The families were almost through Kaze's passage. A worker tripped on the threshold. Jesse caught her. Walter took the child she was carrying and passed him onward.

Arthur moved away from them, down the side of the track until the gun carriage stood between him and the empty spoil pit. He asked a fleeing loader whether anyone worked below it.

“Closed last winter!”

Arthur set his feet.

HIGH NOON changed in his hands, lengthening into THE COUNT. Arthur clicked off the safety and held the trigger.

The charge began as a vibration through the track. A heavy clack marked the round chambering; then that familiar mechanical howl climbed through the yard, setting loose metal trembling.

Ah. That fucking sound again. I'd dearly love to hear it coming from somebody else's country.

Hask saw the rifle and shouted at the gun crew to fire.

Their first burst tore the corner from the loading platform. Stone struck Arthur's coat. His crimson eye remained on the carriage.

The charge reached full.

“Should've let 'em go.”

He fired.

The round drove through the armored carriage, through Hask's cover behind it and into the cutting beyond. The pit wall erupted. A deep channel of broken stone and metal opened behind the impact, carrying the gate, gun and the men serving it into the collapsing spoil.

Arthur's shoulder tore under the recoil. Black tissue closed through the damage while his boots carved backward through the yard. He lowered the weapon with one arm still knitting inside his coat.

Dust rolled over the station.

The firing stopped because there was nothing left at that position capable of continuing it.

Gods above. The man's answer to a locked front door remains a geological event.

On the lower approach, Caitlyn heard the shot through her teeth.

She and Vi had followed the reports of families being moved at gunpoint. They reached the road as a second armed cart came uphill, its crew aiming a mounted weapon toward the workers spilling from the side yard.

Vi shoved an empty wagon across their line. The first rounds punched into its boards.

Caitlyn knelt behind the stone road edge. The new rifle settled against her shoulder. She waited for the mounted gun's support to come clear of the driver and fired.

The powered shot broke the support and drove into the earth bank beyond. The weapon dropped across its crew's knees.

Vi crossed the remaining distance before they freed it. Her gauntlet hit the cart's front frame, turned it sideways and left the men climbing out with their hands raised.

Caitlyn kept them there.

When Sevika arrived from the upper works, she found a vanished gate, surviving guards abandoning their posts and the workers moving away under armed protection.


She took one long look at the ruined gun position.

“Stand down.”

A guard protested.

Sevika struck his rifle barrel toward the ground.

“Did I fucking stutter?”

She went back to tell Silco exactly what he'd lost.

Inside the station, Chris stopped over a fallen guard.

Kaze turned.

“No.”

“He's got a compact tensioner.”

“He also had somewhere to be before you started checking his pockets.”


“Watch is nice too.”

Kaze stared at him.


Teemo said, “Take the tool and get off the fucking body.”

Chris took the tensioner, left the watch and hauled the last useful case toward the passage.

“You people would've left a legendary pelt in a house fire.”

Kaze caught the case with an extra black arm and shoved it through.

“I'd have left you skinning the fucking house.”

Frank stayed with the families until they had a clear route down the road. Caitlyn called to him from the captured cart.

He looked at the prisoners she was guarding, then at the people behind him.

“You gonna keep them out of that box?”

“Yes.”

He held her gaze a moment. Then he backed into the lane and was gone before she could make their unfinished argument the centre of everyone else's escape.

At Renata's workshop, Jesse counted the families as they emerged. Walter counted the cases, stopped himself, then helped a man lower his injured wife onto a bench.

Chris placed the recovered pressure assembly on the floor.

“All right. New kitchen.”

Walter reached toward the main workbench.

Chris put a hand on it first.

“Ground rules haven't changed.”

Walter looked at his hand.

“Nor have mine.”

Jesse dropped into a chair between them.

“Maybe let the people stop bleeding before you measure whose fucking table it is.”

Sevika added what the platform inspectors had reported from the theatre. One enormous shot. A collapsed gallery. A masked body in pieces.

Serve them, or lose the next delivery.

They came through the high windows as the wagon reached the turntable.

A guard swung his rifle toward the first green trail. Ekko saw the muzzle flash and his companion’s board pitch sideways. He pulled the Z-Drive before the falling body struck the rail.

The last few seconds snapped backward around him. Rifle rising. Board passing the window. The same falling fleck of glass beside his wrist.

He came through lower this time, struck the gun aside with his bat and shouted his companion off the original line. The shot broke a pulley above the turntable. Its loose chain whipped across the floor and caught beneath the wagon’s leading wheel, jolting the vehicle sideways.

Jinx saw Ekko through the steel uprights.

Her grin vanished. The next burst followed him instead of Kaze. He dropped beneath the bridge, using the vessel racks for cover, and the Firelights scattered between the cargo.

“Pick a fucking lane!” Sevika shouted up at her.

Jinx ripped the empty feed clear. “He keeps moving!”

The jammed wagon gave Arthur a clear view of the cash chests between its rear braces. He shot the guard reaching for a mounted gun, crossed to the brake lever and found a second man crouching on the far side. The man lunged with a knife. Arthur caught the wrist in his mechanical hand and squeezed until the weapon fell, then drove him into the wheel and put a revolver beneath his chin.

“How’s this brake work?”

The man pointed with his unbroken hand.

“Move it west,” Arthur called.

The trapped chain stretched taut. A link snapped, striking the floor hard enough to spark, and the wagon rolled off the turntable toward the south gate.

On the bridge, a mercenary captain lifted a detonator. A line ran from it to charges strapped around the loading supports. He shouted for everyone to stop.

People did. Even Jinx looked toward the wire.

“You move that money another inch,” he called, “this whole level—”

Kaze pulled him off the bridge.

The captain struck the rail, lost the detonator and came down into Kaze’s waiting hand. Black tissue enclosed the wrist that still clutched the trigger lead. Kaze ripped the arm sideways at the shoulder and drove the man’s head into the side of the wagon. The skull broke against the iron banding. The unfinished threat left his mouth as blood.

The detonator hit the deck above them.

For half a heartbeat, nobody knew whether the fall had been enough.

Then one of the charges blew.

The western support snapped at its base. The loading canopy sagged, hurling dust over the track. His boots slid across the stone until he braced against the turntable pit. Porters scrambled through the space under his arms while the roof pressed down upon him.

Kaze looked up at the broken support, then at the ruined captain in his grip.

“Should’ve started with that.”

He dropped the body and sent a hard gravitational shove into the loose upper framework, pushing its worst weight back . The remaining supports groaned.

There are men who need a lecture before they understand the consequences of impatience. Kaze needed somewhere to put the roof. He considered the two problems much the same once his hand was involved.

One tumbled beneath the wagon. The other drank from a purple vial and came on with a hooked cleaver, his shoulders swelling as the drug took hold. The jaws closed, space wrenching tight at the bite, and the dog’s turn tore the man away from his planted leg. The cleaver fell.

Chris saw the roof sag on the monitor and swore. “Billy, put me out by the south gate.”

“A poor time for a walk.”

“That shooter by the east stair keeps changing angles. I can get him from behind the press.”

Billy moved behind the shelter of a loading vessel, then opened his jaws down past his chest. Chris pulled himself into the outside as the great body folded inward, landing with a stumble and both hands free. His guns came with him. He drew THE CRITIC, settled against the wagon brace and brought the mask’s magnification onto the east stair.

“Left landing,” Teemo said.

“I have eyes.”

“Use the other one. That’s a coat.”

Chris shifted. The real gunman was below the hanging coat, kneeling behind a damaged railing. He fired as the man leaned out. The shot struck beneath the cheek, pitching him against the stair.

“Fine,” Chris muttered.

“What was that?”

“I said fine. Don’t make me fucking thank you twice.”

“You haven’t managed once.”

Chris ducked as a burst chewed the brace beside him. Splinters cut his cheek beneath the edge of the mask. Jinx had found his position. He rolled behind the cash chest, breathing hard, and drew CHOW MAIN when a guard rushed the gap. Two shots dropped the man across the rail. A third attacker appeared above him. Teemo called the movement; Chris fired upward before the barrel cleared the edge, then crawled to a new opening rather than wait for the return burst.

Kaze could have followed the blue-haired gunner. He watched her retreat along the bridge and began lifting his hand toward her next visible position. Then a Firelight crossed below, hauling a crate toward a waiting board, and Chris shouted that somebody was stealing their stolen shit.

Kaze’s attention snapped down.

Ekko landed between him and the Firelight. “Those crates go into the canal.”

“They go where I put them.”

“People are dying because of what’s inside.”

Kaze looked past him at the retreating board. “Then stop carrying it over people.”

Ekko raised the bat as Kaze stepped forward. Before either struck, Arthur called from the wagon. “Money’s moving. You coming or arguing?”

Kaze stared at Ekko, then smiled without warmth. “Take the poison. Touch the cash and see what happens.”

He left for the wagon. Ekko watched him go, one hand close to the Z-Drive, then ordered his people to move the marked crates. The exchange still rang with gunfire. There would be no leisurely inspection of every box.

At the east exit, Sevika dragged a fallen porter clear of the track and forced the smaller reserve chest onto a departing trolley. Jinx dropped from the bridge beside her, landed badly on scattered chain and caught herself against the frame. Blood ran from a shallow cut along her upper arm where a fragment had caught her.

“We’re leaving,” Sevika said.

Jinx looked back toward Ekko’s green trail. Sevika shoved the trolley forward. Beyond it, the east freight tunnel gave them cover from the floor of the exchange. Jinx fired one last burst into the upper supports to keep heads down, then went after her.

Chris watched them disappear and looked at the winch.

Kaze saw him looking.

“Walk away.”

“It’s right there.”

“The roof is falling.”


“I’ve got part of it.”

Daniel cut the taut cable with a sweep of his weapon and kicked it away from the workers still leaving the gate. Chris was already at the winch anchors with a wrench from his kit.

Kaze went very still.

I know that stillness. It is the little grave dug for patience before the shouting starts.

“I can hear you, Mimir.”

“Then perhaps you can hear the roof as well.”

“We came for money,” he said.

Chris strained at the first bolt. “And I found something else.”

“You find something else in every fucking building.”

“Because buildings contain things!”

Arthur rolled the first cash chest toward the gate.

“There,” he said. “Compromise.”

Kaze pointed at him. “You caused this.”

“The bolts? I just solved those.”

Chris put the wrench away with exquisite dignity, then opened his mouth. Billy came out into the dust, took in the freed winch and the two cash chests Arthur had authorized for storage, and swallowed each in turn. The heavy winch went into the space reserved for oversized machinery. The chests joined the useful salvage. A surviving guard who tried to knife Billy during the second swallow found himself going down after the chest, alive and screaming, to a distinctly less profitable destination.

“And the press,” Chris called from inside.

Kaze picked it up first.

“Oh, now you want to carry it?” Chris demanded.

Kaze opened a portal to the high walkway he could see above the south approach and threw the press through. It landed on the intact ledge with a heavy clang, well above any convenient stair.

“Very high shelf,” he said.

Billy gazed up at the ledge with the profound disappointment of a fish denied an appetizer. Chris’s voice from the banjo became so inventive that I learned two new uses for a word I had thought thoroughly exhausted.

They left the exchange with most of the reserve, a winch, two more prisoners and an argument that outlasted the smoke. Behind them, Ekko’s people destroyed the Shimmer they had recovered and withdrew before the Enforcers reached the district. The building still stood, though its loading floor would not carry another wagon without repairs. The men who owned it were going to want payment from someone. I doubted they would start with the dog.

By evening, Caitlyn had the factor’s appointment entry beside a description of the visitor who had used it. The assistant had booked him on a message sent through a freight brokerage and supplied its address. There, the broker’s clerk remembered that same quiet man collecting a sealed payment packet later in the day. He had given no useful name and stayed only long enough to count the amount. She marked the two places on her map and kept the file apart from the furnace superintendent’s death.

Arthur brought the watch to her after she sent word asking about it. Vi waited by the desk, arms folded, while he laid down the cracked enamel case and the theatre ticket.

“Took it off the fellow who took it off your dead man.”

“You kept the chain,” Vi said.

Arthur looked at the bare loop on the case. “Must’ve slipped.”

Caitlyn held out her hand. He considered her for a moment, then laid the chain beside it.

The victim had been identified as a porter who delivered costumes and lamps to several small performance halls. His employer recognized the repaired watch cover. The ticket came from a venue that had closed its public doors months earlier but still rented storage rooms to private clients. Caitlyn turned it under the lamp. Someone had made a fresh ink mark on the back, small and precise.

“You going there?” Arthur asked.

“After we know who rented the rooms.”

“That dye shop was trapped.”

“We recovered the device.”

He nodded toward the ticket. “Then whoever’s doing this likes knowing where folks will put their feet.”

“You recognize the method?”

“I recognize a son of a bitch who wants time to aim.”

Caitlyn copied the storage address for her inquiries. Arthur read it while she wrote. He had come to return a watch, however reluctantly, and left with a place he wanted to see for himself.

Elsewhere, a different man had been given an opportunity to demonstrate his aim over a game of darts.

The drinking house owner had asked him to stop putting holes through the board’s metal backing. A collector took the argument as a chance to demand payment for the damage, then added a fee for the table, the wall and the trouble of explaining himself. Two companions closed the door behind the stranger.

The stranger looked at the sums scratched on the collector’s paper. “You’re making those up.”

The collector drew a knife.

The dart in the stranger’s hand struck him through the eye before the blade cleared his coat. A second dart entered one companion’s throat. The third man grabbed a chair; the stranger caught the falling knife and threw it across the room into his chest. The chair struck the floor over him.

The owner stood behind the bar with both hands raised. The stranger picked up his drink, found a fleck of plaster floating in it and poured it out.

“New glass,” he said.

When the owner’s runner reached Sevika, he brought the collector’s payment sheet and a dart bent where it had struck bone. He described the throws, the distance and the man still sitting in the drinking house after everyone else had left.

“Name?” Sevika asked.

“Someone called him Bullseye. He answered.”

Silco listened from behind his desk. The reserve loss lay itemized before him; beside it sat the cost of repairing the exchange. He turned the bent dart between two fingers, then set it down.

“Find out what he wants. Quietly.”

In the next room, Jinx was binding her cut arm with one hand and her teeth. She could hear every word. When Silco came through, she showed him the torn bounty sheet without looking up.

“Your expensive men broke first.”

“They did.”

“The strangers took your money.”

“Some of it.”

She pulled the knot tight enough to hurt. “And Vi’s still with him.”

Silco sat beside her and reached for the loose end of the bandage. Jinx let him take it after a moment. Neither spoke while he fixed the knot.

Kaze stopped at The Last Drop for a drink and found Vander behind the bar, one hand pressed against his injured ribs. Vi had come back ahead of him. A woman from the market sat near the hearth while someone bound the cut on her calf. The place smelled of boiled cloth beneath the usual beer.

Vander looked at the claim book under Kaze’s arm. “Keep that business outside.”

“I’m buying a drink.”

“Then buy a drink. No prisoners. No stolen cargo. No bounty men dragged in here for questions.”

Kaze stopped at the counter. “You practicing that while I was gone?”

Vi moved away from the hearth. Vander held a hand toward her without taking his eyes off Kaze. His breathing was shallow; standing there cost him something, and the bastard across from him could see exactly how much.

“People come here because they have nowhere else,” Vander said. “They won’t come if they expect a bullet at the door.”

Kaze put a handful of stolen coin on the counter. “Barrel.”

Vander glanced at it, then indicated a small keg by the wall. Vi watched him turn for the door.

“You think paying makes everything yours?” she asked.

Kaze looked back. “No. That was me being polite.”

He left before she could decide what to do with that. “Extra cargo. Slows everybody down.”

“It’s a drink.”

“Chris’s motor was a project.”

Kaze kept walking.

Billy’s banjo erupted with Chris demanding to know what he had missed.

Back inside Billy, Chris resumed Red Dead with his cut cheek cleaned and his temper entirely untreated. He had left the brass press on its ledge.

Teemo watched Chris direct the game’s Arthur toward a stranger standing beside the road.

“You’re going to rob him.”

“He’s got a nice hat.”

“You have a hat.”

Chris slowly turned toward the mask. “You sound like Kaze.”

Outside, Billy’s laughter rolled down the street. Kaze glanced back at him.

“What?”

“Nothing of consequence,” Billy said. “A domestic disagreement.”

“Tell Chris I can reach the shelf.”

Kaze stopped walking.
