Arthur reached the bottom of the hill in time to see the countinghouse door leave its hinges.

The handcart followed it inside.

Kaze had slowed the cart with a hard pull against its motion, sparing the people crossing the street and leaving Chris’s brass press to continue with considerably less restraint. It struck the door at waist height. Daniel stepped off the back rail with his drink intact. Chris arrived among broken wood, payment forms and the abandoned remains of his confidence in communal transport.

“You could have stopped earlier!”

Kaze hopped down. “Could have walked faster.”

Behind the counter, a cashier raised both hands. “We’re closed.”

Chris pulled a splinter from his sleeve. “Your door’s open.”

Two guards reached for their weapons. Arthur shot one through the shoulder and brought his other revolver to bear on the second. The second guard laid his gun carefully on the floor. I admired his flexibility under changing market conditions.

Kaze dropped the bounty notice on the counter. “Who pays this?”

“The factor.”

“Get him.”

The cashier looked toward the little office behind the wire partition. A boot protruded from its doorway.

Kaze went through. The factor sat crooked beneath his own desk with a single wound in his forehead. There was very little blood on the desktop and rather more gathering beneath his head. His safe stood closed. His signet ring remained on his hand.

Somebody had reached him first.

Less than an hour earlier, the man now lying under the desk had admitted a quiet courier carrying a sealed business envelope. His morning appointment book contained a matching entry. The courier had waited for the clerk to leave with a stack of transfer slips, stepped inside and closed the door.

“You’re early,” the factor had said.

“You asked for discretion.”

Forty-seven placed the envelope on the desk. It contained copies of freight insurance claims the factor had sold twice. His client, an importer whose company would have carried the resulting losses, had supplied those copies through the broker from the freight clerks’ referral. A deposit, the target’s portrait, the address, the appointment routine. Enough to assess the work. The importer had asked for a death, not a public lesson.

The factor looked at the first page, reached beneath the desk and met the muzzle of a suppressed pistol. The shot was a short, ugly cough in the small room. Forty-seven caught the falling body before it struck the cabinet, lowered it and checked the pulse. Then he recovered the papers.

He left while the cashier was arguing with a messenger about whether a seal was authentic. Nobody stopped a courier who had already been admitted. By the time an assistant found the body, he had changed his outer coat in a disused service room and was walking toward the broker’s agreed drop.

Now Kaze stared at the factor’s neat wound with the offended expression of a man who had arrived at a feast to find somebody had eaten his portion.

Chris crouched beside the desk. Teemo switched the mask’s view back from magnification after examining the wound.

“Close,” Teemo said. “He sat still for it.”

“Until he didn’t.” Chris checked beneath the desk and found the factor’s untouched pistol in a holster fixed to the wood. “Well, hello.”

Kaze turned. “Leave it.”

“Evidence.”

“You didn’t give a fuck about evidence until it had a trigger.”

“He should preserve the holster too. Complete picture.”

Chris pointed at him. “Exactly.”

“Could document the desk.”

“I hate both of you,” Kaze said.

In the front room, the cashier was explaining that most of the reserve had already left for the freight exchange. A runner had arrived with an urgent order to move the remaining claim money, found the factor dead and shown the existing transfer authority to the senior clerk. The clerk had taken that last satchel onto the lower freight lift. Arthur found the lift gate open over an empty shaft.

“They’ve got a head start.”

Kaze looked down through the metal grating. Far below, lamplight moved with the descending platform. He opened a portal onto the visible deck.

The guard on it had enough time to raise his rifle. Kaze caught the barrel and pushed it upward as the shot went into the shaft wall. His right arm thickened around the weapon, dragged the man close and drove an elbow through the front of his face. The second guard fired across the platform. Kaze shoved the first body into the bullets and crossed behind it.

Upstairs, the lift’s handbrake handle began hammering against its housing. Chris saw the cable jerk. “Get off that fucking thing!”

The frightened clerk at the controls had pulled the release too far. The overloaded platform dropped, shuddering down its guide rails. Kaze grabbed the money satchel from the clerk’s shoulder, caught the control frame with his other hand and tore it from the deck. The mechanism shrieked as the brake bit unevenly.

At the landing below, a dockworker looked up into the descending mass.

He dragged the worker out by the collar and stepped beneath the platform’s edge, catching it across both forearms as its corner struck the landing. The impact punched cracks through the masonry under his feet.

It came down with a crash that shook dust out of three floors. The surviving guard lost his footing. Kaze hit him before he could recover, driving his skull against the steel frame. The clerk rolled beneath the railing and fled along the lower passage, his empty shoulder strap trailing behind him.

“Daniel,” Kaze called through the shaft. “Clerk!”

Daniel was already moving, bare feet pattering along the upper walkway. He stepped over its rail, caught a pipe with his tail and swung down to the next level, landing ahead of the fleeing man.

“I only handle the freight payments!” the clerk shouted.

“Terrible news,” he said. “We’re auditing.”

The clerk threw a bundle of transfer slips into Daniel’s face and tried to get past. Daniel let the papers scatter, hooked the man’s ankle with the butt of his spear and sat him down hard. Then he crouched to gather the slips while the clerk wheezed.

From the adjoining stair, a cable snapped around the bundle and pulled it out of Daniel’s hand.

Daniel looked up. Daredevil stood at the top of the short flight, one arm held close against his bruised ribs. The collector had described the dock robbery before giving him directions to this building. Matt had followed them, heard the wreckage inside and reached the lower passage in time to hear the fleeing clerk identify himself. Paper rasped beneath his glove as he tucked the bundle inside his suit.

“You’re keeping those men alive,” Matt said.

“You’re keeping my paperwork.” Daniel rose, taking a measured drink. “One of these is easier to fix.”

Matt backed toward the stair door. Daniel’s spear lengthened across the passage and shut it before he reached it. Matt struck the shaft aside, lunged under it and drove a club toward Daniel’s wrist. Daniel turned his forearm into ice. The blow chipped it. His other hand caught Matt’s elbow while his tail hooked the ankle behind him.

Matt twisted out of the first grip, using the stair rail to keep his weight beneath him. Daniel let him. He swayed backward like a drunk losing a fight with the floor, then stepped inside the next swing and tapped Matt beneath the chin with the heel of his hand. Matt’s teeth snapped together. His second club came across low. Daniel caught it between his foot and the stair, pinned it and pushed Matt against the rail with the spear shaft.

“You smell like a distillery,” Matt said through the pressure.

“Family resemblance.”

Matt tried to wrench the shaft away. Daniel increased the pressure just enough to stop him. The red mask turned toward the clerk, who was crawling along the opposite wall.

“Let him leave.”

“He can leave when he tells me where the bags were going.”

“You took Shimmer from the docks.”

“Stole it. Different invoice.”

“You expect me to believe that makes you better?”

Daniel’s grin faded into something cooler. “I expect you to stop deciding what I said before I finish saying it.”

The clerk reached beneath his coat. Matt heard the leather scrape and turned toward him. Daniel saw the pistol through the folded cloth before it emerged. A flick of the spear knocked the muzzle aside; the shot broke a stair spindle. Daniel drove the butt into the clerk’s temple, dropping him against the wall, then took Matt’s papers back while Matt was still trying to reach the weapon.

“There,” Daniel said. “Still alive. You can put that one on your tab.”

Matt swung at him. Daniel caught the wrist, turned him across the rail and held him there, feet barely finding the step below. The lad’s breathing had become a ragged business. Daniel studied him for a moment, then released him toward the stairs instead of over them.

“Kaze do that to your ribs?”

Matt steadied himself against the wall. “You know him.”

“I know you’re not going to lie down just because it hurts.” Daniel tucked the slips into his belt. “But you are going to fall down if you keep this up.”

He took the pistol from the unconscious clerk, emptied it and tossed it into the shaft. Matt knelt beside the man as Daniel walked away. Behind the red mask, Matt’s mouth was bleeding. He pressed two fingers to the clerk’s neck and waited until he was certain of the pulse.

Daniel called back without turning. “Freight transfer. Sixth bell. If you heard me read it, you might remember it.”

Matt looked up, but the barefoot man had already gone around the corner. An insult, a warning and a usable fact in the same breath. Daniel could be generous in ways that made you want to hit him again.

“You volunteering, Mimir?”

I most certainly was not. The lad took another drink and continued downstairs, thoroughly pleased with himself.

By the time Caitlyn reached the countinghouse, the group had left with the money, the claim records and the transfer slips. They had also left the factor’s body, the surviving cashier, a smashed lift and an empty space beneath the desk where a pistol and its holster had been.

“We heard gunfire after the cart,” the cashier told her. “But he was already dead.”

“Who found him?”

“His assistant. Before they arrived.”

Caitlyn examined the office. The shot had come from in front of the desk, close enough for the target to be seated almost directly beneath its final path. The guard killed on the lower platform had suffered a very different end. She took statements separately, including the courier’s brief visit and the time written beside his appointment.

Vi stood outside the partition while Caitlyn worked. “Think it’s the one from the dye shop?”

“That man was arranged to be found. This one was left where he fell.” Caitlyn looked at the appointment book. “I want the person who entered this name.”

The earlier visitor’s careful work lay beneath a later avalanche of broken timber and blood. Untangling the two would take patience. Fortunately, Caitlyn had brought her own; Kaze had certainly left none behind.

At the cold-store workshop, Chris finally got his stolen brake assembly onto a bench.

Billy had spat it out beside the rear loading door, then returned Chris to the outside in another wet inversion that caused the proprietor to retreat into his own storeroom. Kaze dropped into a chair and opened the money satchel. There was enough in it to make the morning profitable, though far less than the bounty’s advertised total.

“Installments,” Arthur said.

Kaze counted another stack. “Cheap motherfucker.”

Chris had sent a runner to Jayce and Viktor with a tracing of the assembly’s maker’s mark and an offer to let them examine it. By the time they arrived, he had removed the cover and laid its linkage beside the salvaged rifle receiver, three drawer runners and the brass press. Teemo was describing the bench as an excellent place for an ambush because nobody could see the fucking bench.

“Keep talking,” Chris told him. “I’ll put you in a doorbell.”

“You couldn’t reverse the last thing he did to me.”

The screwdriver stopped for half a second. Across the room, Kaze continued counting. Chris set the tool down more carefully than the conversation deserved.

“I’m trying to figure out this component. You can help or you can haunt the fucking screwdriver.”

Teemo’s voice came lower. “There’s a crack beside the rear mount.”

Chris bent closer. There was.

Jayce saw the exposed unit and stopped at the bench. “Where did you get that?”

“Dock.”

“Which dock?”

Kaze looked up. “Ours, briefly.”

Viktor leaned on his cane to examine the housing. “This is an industrial regulator. Or it began as one.” He indicated a modified mounting collar. “Someone has forced the drive to accommodate a load it was never designed to carry.”

Chris pointed at the compact blue-lit part. “That’s what I wanted you to look at.”

Jayce reached for it. Chris caught his wrist.

“Ask.”

“You asked me here.”

“To look. You’re looking with your fucking hands.”

“Careful. He’s sensitive about people taking things.”

Arthur laughed into his cup. Chris aimed a finger at him without looking away from Jayce.

“You shut up. I know what’s in your pockets.”

“More now than this morning.”

Viktor settled the argument by asking for a probe and holding his hand out until Chris supplied one. Under the work lamp, he traced a hairline fracture running from the overloaded mount. The component still held charge. Its safety housing had been bypassed to keep the freight brake operating under heavier loads.

“If you energize it here,” Viktor said, “you may lose the bench.”

“I hadn’t connected it.”

Jayce pointed to a lead clipped at the edge of the assembly.

“Test ground,” Chris said. “Other end’s loose. Try following it before you start the fucking speech.”

Jayce followed it. It was loose. He set it down and took a breath. “Then let us isolate it properly.”

“Us?”

“You wanted help.”

Kaze tipped his chair back. “He wanted somebody to tell him his garbage was special.”

“Your bell is in my house.”

“And?”

“It could become a toilet bell.”

Jayce looked from one man to another, visibly reconsidering the decisions that had brought him there.

Chris’s expression changed when Jayce identified a stamped serial range as one issued to a licensed Piltover distributor. Kaze set his chair on all four legs. The altered unit had reached a Shimmer dock through a supplier who could be named. On the transfer slips Daniel had recovered, that same distributor’s mark appeared beside the evening’s reserve movement: goods and cash going through the old freight exchange.

“There,” Kaze said, tapping the paper. “We take that one too.”

Jayce stared at the blood dried along its edge. “You can’t keep raiding every building connected to this.”

“Watch me.”

“Workers use those buildings.”

“Then tell your distributor to stop loading people’s problems into them.”

Viktor looked , who had gone quieter. “How much damage was done at the dock?”

“And they’re moving through an occupied exchange now.”

Kaze stood. Waiting for a sixth bell had become less appealing with every word. He wanted the reserve, the supplier and something more satisfying than a dead accountant. He folded the transfer slip and took the bounty notice from Arthur.

“Then we go early.”

Across the district, the same disrupted freight system had brought Walter White a problem he found considerably more interesting than cleaning stock. His employer’s supplier arrived with a cloudy liquid in a sealed sample bottle and an angry demand for a substitute processing wash. A previous shipment had been stolen, the next delayed by the furnace closure, and the workshop would be paid if its two newcomers could produce something that behaved consistently.

Walter held the bottle against the light. “You want consistency. That starts with telling me what this has been exposed to.”

The supplier objected to questions. Walter put the bottle down.

“Then find someone willing to guess.”

Jesse watched the man decide how much the delay was costing him. At last he named the equipment, the heat conditions and the residue the wash was supposed to remove. Walter asked for three ordinary samples from the line and refused to work from the one the supplier had selected to impress him. It was a small insistence, but I have watched empires fare worse than men who know exactly which question they need answered.

Later, when the supplier had gone, Jesse stopped Walter beside the worktable.

“That kid out back. The coughing. This stuff’s from the same place.”

“We’re improving a cleaning process.”

“That’s what you’re calling it.”

Walter put on his spectacles. “Would you prefer they keep exposing people to an unstable process?”

Jesse looked at the bottle, then at the closed door. “I’d prefer you didn’t make that sound like I asked you to poison somebody.”

Their improved sample left the shop in a padded box before evening. Its carrier passed it to a second man, who took it through a guarded door to Singed. Beside the physician’s table, Deckard’s remains lay beneath a stained covering. Singed listened to the report, tested a drop from the new bottle and asked who had insisted on the additional samples.

“An older man. Foreign. Calls himself White.”

Singed looked again at the test. “Bring me his observations. In his own words.”

No praise, no invitation yet. Just a new name written where he would see it again.

At the freight exchange, Sevika had ordered the cash loaded behind a consignment of spare pressure vessels. Jinx stood on the upper maintenance bridge with a bundle of wire over one shoulder. Below her, porters rolled the vessels into place while guards argued about the men who had already failed to collect the bounty.

“You’re keeping the approach clear,” Sevika told her. “Not demolishing the fucking exchange.”

Jinx glanced down. “You say the sweetest things.”

She followed the wire to a small release mechanism fixed above the loading track. Beyond the exchange’s high windows, a masked Firelight crouched on a roof, watching the cargo marks. He had followed one of Silco’s surviving barges from the lower dock, then the wagons that met it. He left when the first pressure vessel rolled under the bridge, carrying the route back to Ekko.

Inside Billy, Chris returned to his railway business while the others took the approach to the exchange on foot. The damaged regulator remained at the workshop under a locked cover; its measurements travelled with Jayce and Viktor. Through the second monitor, Chris watched Kaze walk ahead, apparently deciding which door most deserved to become a hole.

“He’s going to break the freight equipment,” Chris said.

Teemo’s answer was immediate. “Probably.”

“We should get there first.”

“You could stop playing.”

Chris moved his horse off the track. “You could stop being a dick.”

“Big winch by the south loading door. Looked expensive on the map.”

Kaze heard him.

“Just helping him prepare.”

From somewhere inside that enormous fish came the sound of a game being paused with tremendous purpose.

Chris was trying to rob a train when somebody outside offered to buy his head.

An awkward overlap of business interests, aye.

He had gone back inside Billy after breakfast, leaving the others to walk him to the cold-store workshop while he attended to what he called an urgent railway matter. On one monitor, Chris was backing onto a railway track while demanding a passenger’s valuables. On the other, through Billy’s hat, a little man in a leather apron was holding up a freshly printed bounty sheet.

“Hold that still,” Chris said through the banjo.

The printer obeyed. Billy’s smile encouraged cooperation in much the same way an open grave encouraged careful footing. There were six rough likenesses on the paper, with an additional fish-headed sketch beside Chris’s. Arthur’s looked like a debt collector who had recently eaten another debt collector. Kaze had been given two matching eyes and a shirt.


“That’s not my fucking nose,” Kaze said.

Chris pressed the video pedal with his heel, freezing the picture while his thumbs kept working. “Zoom the paper toward your face, Billy. I can’t read the bottom.”

“You have arrested the picture, Christopher. I could insert the gentleman into my nostril and it would remain the same picture.”

Teemo spoke from the mask beside Chris’s chair. “Train’s moving.”

“I know the train’s moving.”

“You’re standing on the track.”

The first monitor furnished a practical demonstration. Chris stared at the red death screen, then at the Predator mask.

“You waited until the fucking train was touching me.”

“You said you knew.”

“Big money. You should get a copy for the wall.”

“I’ll get the original artist for the wall.”

The printer’s smile departed. Arthur took the sheet before Kaze could turn criticism into a trade dispute. A verification mark occupied the bottom corner, above a payment address in the lower commercial tier. The sum was enough to change a family’s life. Enough to make a competent man foolish, and a foolish man load both barrels.

“They’re paying for the dog too,” Arthur said.

Kaze watched people recognize them. A stallholder pulled his shutters halfway down. Two men at a drinking stand left their cups and walked in different directions.

“Good,” Kaze said. “Now we don’t have to find them.”

“We were finding a workshop,” Chris complained.

“You’re playing cowboy in a fish.”

Arthur folded the sheet. “He’s what?”

“Nothing,” Chris said, far too promptly.

Their intended route had already changed. The furnace crossing was shut behind a cordon, and freight that usually passed below the shops had been diverted through the market. A crane operator swore at a wagon driver. A woman swore at both. Beyond the cordon, soot-blackened workers were carrying a stretcher with a coat over it.

The dead man beneath the coat was a tariff superintendent whose portrait had appeared in yesterday’s paper. His full name had accompanied a proud announcement about stricter collections. There had also been a smaller account of three workers imprisoned after refusing his private surcharge.

Light had read both.

Hours earlier, in the room he had rented, he had copied the superintendent’s name while keeping the printed face in view. The instructions beneath it were spare: burn the private collection ledger in the furnace at the start of the shift, then fall into the open service pit while leaving. Light checked the time against the clock on the wall and closed the notebook.

Ryuk leaned over the newspaper. “That one collected money.”

“He imprisoned people who couldn’t pay him.”

“You didn’t meet them.”

Light straightened the paper’s crease. “I don’t need a personal introduction to recognize abuse of power.”

Ryuk’s laugh scraped through the room. “Lucky for everybody.”

At the furnace, the superintendent had dismissed his assistant, fed the ledger into the heat and, minutes later, stepped through a gap beside the maintenance rail. The assistant heard the impact. Now the crossing was closed, the accounts were ash, and half the market’s morning traffic was trapped above it. Light watched the commotion from an upstairs window with the notebook hidden away. The people below were already inventing reasons for what had happened.

Kaze’s group met the diverted freight halfway up the market.

Billy paused beside a wagon carrying a dismantled industrial sewing machine. Its motor housing sat exposed between sacks of thread. Chris’s foot struck the pedal again.

“Back up.”

Kaze kept walking. “No.”

“I wasn’t talking to you.”

“You’re about to make it everybody’s problem.”

“That bracket might fit the dock brake.”

Chris nearly came through the banjo. “Exactly. Thank you. Somebody has a fucking brain.”

“Could take hours if the bolts are seized.”

“You tall, messy bastard.”

“I’m supporting local engineering.”

Billy bent over the motor. The wagon driver began explaining that it belonged to someone else. Above him, in a second-floor room, a crossbow settled on the back of Kaze’s head.

Kaze followed the movement, saw the weapon, and pulled.

The shooter came through the shutters shoulder-first. Wood burst over the street. His bolt discharged into the wall as Kaze dragged him down, caught him by the throat and drove him into the cobbles. The man’s skull struck hard enough to end the conversation before it began.

For a breath, the market held still around the body. Then a whistle shrilled from behind the freight wagons, and the waiting crew opened fire.

Arthur shot the first rifleman before his muzzle had cleared the side of a cart. He folded the barrel sideways and rammed the stock into its owner’s mouth. Teeth struck the pavement. Another hunter lunged at his knee with a hooked blade

Inside Billy, the game continued without Chris. He had dropped the controller when the first shot cracked. “Left, by the awning. Gun under the blue cloth.”

Billy turned as the cloth fell. A stubby scattergun fired into his chest at close range. He rocked back a step, looked down at the torn fabric and wet punctures, then looked at the gunman.

“You have put considerable effort into spoiling my morning.”

The banjo struck the man’s forearm with a crack, knocking the gun loose. Billy’s other hand closed around his coat. His jaws spread, the head widening with them, and the man vanished into a wet, panicked gulp. A boot scraped Billy’s lip. Then even that was gone.

“Could’ve got the gun too,” Chris said.

“I could have swallowed your chair.”

“Hostile workplace.”

On the far side of the wagon, Daniel let a knife pass beside his ear, caught the attacker’s wrist with his tail and turned under it. The joint broke as he stepped through. He plucked a falling bottle from the man’s coat with his bare foot, caught it in his hand, read the label and made a disappointed noise.

“Rubbing alcohol. Your evening was already ruined.”

His spear extended through the second attacker before the fellow could use the opening. Daniel withdrew it, kicked the collapsing body away from a fleeing shopkeeper and ducked beneath the wagon to reach the next gunman.

Kaze had crossed to the whistle. Its owner retreated between two stalls, firing a pistol as he ran. One round struck Kaze high in the chest; black tissue closed around the wound while he kept advancing. The man saw it happen. His second shot went wild.

“That was your good idea?” Kaze asked.

The pistol lifted again. Kaze caught the wrist, bent the arm backward across its owner’s shoulder and drove him face-first into a butcher’s block. Bone snapped beneath his palm. He left him there and turned toward the upper balcony, where a rifle was tracking Arthur.

A black, narrow blade grew into Kaze’s right hand as he drew across his body from the brief sheath at his left hip. The portal he opened faced the balcony he could see. He stepped through beside the rifleman and cut before the man could turn. Blood struck the rail. The rifle fell into the street, followed by its owner.

Chris’s voice rose from below. “Catch that!”

Kaze looked at the falling weapon and let it hit the stones.

“You fucking saw it!”

“Saw that too.”

The last two hunters tried the alley behind the fish stalls. Arthur put a round through the other man’s leg and caught his coat as he fell.

“Where’s the whistle man getting paid?”

The hunter looked past Arthur at Kaze, now stepping out of the portal with BlackMarrow sliding back into his hand.

“Collection office. Red door. Under the freight stairs.”

“How many?”

“I don’t—”

Arthur pressed a boot against the wounded leg. The man supplied a more useful estimate.

I have known governments founded on less persuasive consultation.

By the time Chris came back outside, pushing through Billy’s yawning, inside-out mouth in a revolting exchange of flesh and ownership, the market was empty except for the injured, the dead and three traders shouting about damage. His sleeve still bore yesterday’s tear. He checked the dressing on his arm, drew CHOW MAIN in his right hand and hurried to the fallen rifle.

Kaze stepped on it.

“Move your fucking foot.”

“We’re leaving.”

“That’s a custom receiver.”

“You have guns.”

“Looks rare.”

“Stop helping him,” Kaze said.

“Might be worthless. Hard to tell without taking it apart.”

Chris looked between them. “You’re doing this on purpose.”

Kaze lifted his foot only when Chris shoved the receiver into his bag and abandoned the splintered stock. They had wasted perhaps ten seconds. Kaze resented every one of them with the concentration another man might reserve for a blood feud.

Arthur took a watch from the hunter with the wounded leg. It had a cracked enamel cover and a theatre ticket folded around its chain. The man reached for it, then remembered the boot.

“Yours?” Arthur asked.

“Found it.”

“Where?”

“Empty dye shop. By the old tram turn. There was a man in a chair.”

Arthur stopped winding the chain around his hand.

“Dead man?”

The hunter nodded. “I only took the watch.”

Arthur pocketed both watch and ticket. Kaze was already heading downhill, expecting the rest to follow. The dog left the butcher’s block reluctantly. Aye, there are appetites even I prefer not to examine before lunch.

The new prisoner inside Billy had landed beside the two dock guards and the mechanic. One guard recognized the bounty sheet protruding from his pocket, read the figure and accused him of accepting a lower rate than the dock crew’s promised bonus. The newcomer accused the guard of getting eaten for free. Their argument became a fight over the paper. The mechanic took the opportunity to move his bedding farther from all three.

Below the market, the collection office was already closing.

Matt Murdock had reached it before the shooting. The shop assistant he had protected the previous night had described a collector’s damaged voice and the chain he wore at his waist. Matt had followed that voice from a collection stop to the red door. Now, from the narrow service passage behind it, he could hear coins being swept into a bag and a frightened clerk insisting that he had only copied the notices.

“Then copy yourself a fucking excuse,” the collector rasped.

A slap. A chair overturned. Matt’s hand closed around his billy club.

The front door burst inward before he reached the rear one.

Kaze took the collector’s armed guard by the face and drove him into the wall. The pistol fired against the ceiling. Plaster fell over the desk as the man slid down it. Chris ducked behind the broken door and shot a second guard reaching beneath his coat. Arthur covered the stairs.

The collector threw the money bag at Kaze and ran for the service passage. Matt met him at the rear threshold, stripped the knife from his hand and put him down with two hard blows. Then Kaze walked through the office and reached for him.

Matt’s club caught the outstretched wrist.

Kaze looked at the club, then the red mask above it. A slow grin exposed gold over silver.

“Daredevil.”

Matt heard no surprise in the voice. “Back away from him.”

“He just paid people to shoot at us.”

“Then he can answer for it.”

Kaze glanced at the bleeding collector. “That’s what I came to do.”

Matt moved when Kaze reached again, striking the elbow and turning his body to throw him away from the man on the floor. Kaze let the joint bend. Too far. Wrongly. Black tissue shifted beneath Matt’s grip, and Kaze’s hand closed around the back of his neck.

He drove Matt through the rear doorway into the passage. Matt’s shoulder struck brick. He rolled with it, kicked at Kaze’s knee and whipped the club toward his temple. Kaze caught the weapon, yanked him forward by its cable and hit him once in the ribs.

The breath left Matt in a harsh burst. He stayed upright long enough to catch the return wrist and turn aside from a second blow. Kaze simply followed him. There was no yielding weight to exploit, no human hesitation between commitment and impact. He put Matt against the wall with his forearm across the chest and lifted until the boots scraped clear of the ground.

“You came all the way down here,” Kaze said, “to stand in front of this piece of shit?”

Matt drove his forehead into Kaze’s face. Blood ran from Kaze’s nose, and the nose straightened as he smiled.

“All right.”

He threw Matt across the passage. The red suit struck a stack of empty crates, breaking them under him. The collector crawled toward the open drain while Matt forced air back into his lungs. Kaze turned, hooked the man by the ankle and dragged him through the spilled rubbish.

“Where’s the actual money?”

“Countinghouse. Upper intake. I just register claims.”

“Whose account?”

“I don’t see the account.”

Kaze planted a foot on his hand. The collector screamed. Matt pushed himself out of the crates and sent the club’s cable around Kaze’s ankle, hauling sideways. Kaze barely shifted, but the foot came off the trapped fingers.

“Persistent little fucker, aren’t you?”

“You have what you need.” Matt’s breathing scraped around the bruised ribs. “Let him go.”

“You don’t know what I need.”

There it was, brother: the irritation sharpening into pleasure because somebody had finally given it a face. Kaze had a destination. The man under him could scarcely hold a pen. Yet his attention stayed on the wounded devil dragging himself upright, still trying to make the same impossible intervention.

“You’ve already won,” Matt said.

Kaze’s smile thinned. “And?”

He pulled Matt straight off his feet with a sharp gravitational tug, caught him by the front of the suit and slammed him against the wall beside the collector. This time Matt’s knees folded when Kaze released him. Chris appeared in the doorway, pistol ready, then lowered it as he took in the passage.

“Holy shit. Is that—”

“Yes,” Kaze said.

“Does he have anything good?”

Even I needed a moment with that one.

“Chris,” I said, “the man can hardly breathe.”

“I meant the asshole on the ground.”

“There are several candidates.”

Kaze laughed. Matt used the breath he had recovered to speak to the clerk hiding behind the door. “Go. Now.”

The clerk ran past Chris. Kaze watched him, then crouched in front of Matt, close enough for the blood on his knuckles to drip onto the red suit.

“Keep him,” he said, nodding toward the collector. “Next time you put your hands on me, bring a better reason.”

Matt lifted his head. “He was reason enough.”

Kaze regarded him for another heartbeat. Then he stood, took the collector’s key ring and walked back through the office. Leaving the man alive had become his decision, and he wore it with all the generosity of a king returning a tooth after an extraction.

“Your friend?”

“Nosy.”

Chris had already opened a drawer. “You took longer than my fucking rifle.”

“He’s got you there.”

Kaze looked at them both. “I will put everything you own on a very high shelf.”

“That’s discrimination,” Chris said.

Arthur returned from the stairs carrying a claim book. “Money ain’t here. Names are. Let’s quit jawing before somebody moves both.”

That reached Kaze where moral instruction had failed. He snatched the book, found the countinghouse stamp on its first page and headed out. Behind them, Matt knelt beside the collector and bound the damaged hand with the man’s own scarf. The collector flinched at every touch.

“I need a name,” Matt said.

“He asked that.”

“I’m asking you.”

The difference cost Matt another painful breath. He waited for the answer.

By midday, Caitlyn had three new statements, two different locations full of bodies and a superintendent’s accidental death with a very deliberate fire immediately before it. The furnace assistant sat across from her, twisting his cap.

“He burned the private book?” she asked.

“Watched it catch. Made me fetch more fuel.”

“Was anyone threatening him?”

“He was the one doing the threatening.”

Caitlyn set that account beside the earlier unexplained deaths, leaving the market killings on another part of the desk. Marcus entered while she was marking the time. His coat had been brushed clean, though fatigue had settled deeper than dust could.

“You’re to concentrate on the armed disturbances.”

“I am. I also have a witness to the destruction of financial evidence.”

“A man fell.”

“After burning a ledger in front of his assistant.”

Marcus looked at the statement. “Then record that.”

He left without asking for the witness. Caitlyn watched the doorway, then told the assistant to stay until an escort could take him home. Outside her office, Vi waited with a description Arthur had passed through a runner: old tram turn, empty dye shop, a dead man seated inside.

They went together. The shutters were closed from within, but a side entrance stood ajar. Through it, Caitlyn saw a chair placed under a hanging lamp. Dried blood had been worked into the arrangement of pale cloth around its occupant. His wrist was bare where a watch had shielded the skin. The lamp’s light fell across a wound dressed in petals.

Vi took a step forward. Caitlyn caught her sleeve.

“Look at the floor.”

A fine wire crossed between two boards beside the chair. Vi stopped. From the threshold, Caitlyn could see that the body had been moved, supported and positioned with care. She sent for tools and kept everyone outside.

I have seen men decorate a hall after a victory. Whoever had prepared that room had begun with the decoration and found himself a man to finish it.

Across the lower district, a paid runner finally reached Sevika with news from the market. She listened through the casualties, the swallowed hunter and the broken collection office. When the runner described Kaze walking out with the claim book, she reached for her coat.

Silco stopped her at the door. “Warn the factor. Move the reserve.”

“And the crews still looking for them?”

“Let them discover what the price requires.”

In the adjoining room, Jinx had spread one of the bounty sheets beside an opened pistol. A charcoal line circled the dog, another the huge man beside it. She ignored both and drew a small pair of boxing gloves beside Kaze’s likeness. Then she rubbed the drawing away so hard that the paper tore.

Down by the intake stairs, Kaze found an empty freight handcart and kicked the brake free. Chris was carrying a small brass press from the collection office. Teemo had spent the last street telling him it was heavy, conspicuous and likely useless.

“It stamps the payment slips,” Chris snapped. “We might need it.”

“You took the drawer runners too.”

“Precision steel.”

“He could stamp our own bounty claims.”

Kaze stopped with one hand on the handle. He looked at the press, then the claim book, then Chris.

“Get on.”

“Why?”

“You wanted your shit. Bring your shit.”

Arthur stepped clear of the wheels. Daniel hopped onto the back rail, bottle in hand.

Chris grabbed the brass press with one arm and the rail with the other. “This thing has a brake, right?”

“Had one,” Arthur said.

The cart dropped over the slope. Kaze jumped aboard, grinning, and Chris’s answer chased them all the way down the hill.

The guard Arthur had brought back was bleeding through his shirt again.

He sat beneath the rear window of The Last Drop with his ruined hand pressed against his chest. Every few breaths he looked at the door, measured the distance, then looked at Arthur.

“You can try,” Arthur said.

The man stayed seated.

Inside, the physician wanted light. Chris gave him the headlamp. He wanted room. He wanted everyone to stop answering questions meant for Vander, and Vi managed that one with considerably more difficulty.

Kaze came into the yard while the doctor was examining the bruising beneath Vander’s ribs.

“Where’s the money go?”

The guard stared at him.

“What?”

“The money. The purple shit. All of it.”

“I watch a door.”

Arthur flicked ash away from the wounded hand.

“Watched it open, too. Try remembering what went through.”

The man swallowed.

“Transfer dock. Under the old pumping sheds. Barges take it from there.”

“Silco there?” Kaze asked.

“Sometimes. I don’t know.”

The red pattern in Kaze’s right eye held his attention. Whatever else he saw in that gaze, it made the next answer come quickly.

“I haven’t seen him there today. I swear.”

Kaze crouched, keeping their eyes level.

“Then tell me something you have seen.”

The guard supplied a route from the room where they’d found Vander, a painted wheel above a loading entrance, and a foreman with a steel brace on his left leg. He’d carried meals down there. He knew which bell meant a barge was ready. Beyond that, terror had nothing useful left to offer.

Kaze stood.

Arthur looked toward the bar.

“What’re you thinking?”

“Take his shit.”

Chris had reached the doorway in time to hear that.

“What kind of shit?”

There he was. The lad could hear opportunity through masonry.

—

Sevika found Deckard’s body in the passage beneath the pumping sheds.

She looked at the cracked wall, the crushed shotgun, and the head lying apart from the body. Then she turned to the guard who’d fled the stairs.

“They take anything?”

“Vander. One of ours.”

“Which one?”

He told her.

Sevika swore.

“He knows the lower dock. Move the cash and the finished stock. Everything else waits.”

The foreman began an objection about the loading schedule.

She stepped close enough that the metal fingers of her left hand touched his ledger.

“The schedule just had its fucking head cut off.”

He shut the book.

Sevika sent a runner ahead to Silco, stayed long enough to see the first cart move, then left by the upper passage. Below her, bells rang out of their ordinary order. Men began arguing about which crates had priority.

Fear can move a great deal of cargo. Rarely neatly.

—

Vi caught Kaze beside the bar.

“Where are you going?”

“Dock.”

“I’m coming.”

From the next room, Vander coughed. The physician called her name.

She turned toward the sound, furious at having to choose.

The doctor had finally given the man something for the pain and told Arthur to stop interrogating him until the bleeding was controlled.

“We know the way.”

Vi looked at Kaze.

“If you find Silco—”

“I’ll know who he is.”

“That’s not what I was going to say.”

Kaze waited.

Her jaw tightened.

“Don’t let him talk you into anything.”

That earned a small grin.

Chris checked THE CRITIC’s sling and pulled the mask down over his face. Its metal sections seated around his headlamp with a brief rattle and the alien chirp he still enjoyed hearing.

Teemo appeared in the corner of his vision, red lenses turned toward the door.

“What are we taking?”

“We’ll see.”

“That’s how people end up carrying explosives.”

“Billy’s good with explosives.”

“You’re not Billy.”

Chris checked the release on his mask.

“I fucking noticed.”

—

They returned through Kaze’s opening to the room where Vander had been held.

The chair was still there. So was the smell.

Daniel took a drink and passed beneath a low pipe, bare toes gripping the edge of a raised channel. His spear shortened in his hand to clear the turn.

“Left,” he said.

Arthur glanced at him.

“Sign?”

Daniel’s pale eyes tracked through the nearer wall.

“People moving boxes. Very nervous boxes.”

They followed the passage down.

The loading entrance stood open beneath a wheel painted white. Beyond it lay a stone quay, two barges, and a winch lowering a sling of crates toward the water. Men worked under yellow lamps. Armed guards occupied the upper rail and the narrow bridge between the sheds.

Chris stopped beside a stack of empty drums.

In his mask, Teemo marked a man whose hand rested on a belt-fed gun mounted above the nearest loading lane.

“That one first if he turns it.”

“I see him.”

Kaze walked through the entrance.

The foreman with the leg brace looked up.

“Loading crew’s through the other—”

He saw the black flesh on Kaze’s right side.


His mouth stayed open.

Kaze looked at the crates, the money box chained beneath the foreman’s table, and the guards moving along the rail.

“Leave that.”

The foreman’s hand went toward a whistle.

Arthur already had a revolver out.

“Wouldn’t.”

From above, someone shouted that they were the ones from the holding rooms.

The gunner swung his weapon.

Chris fired THE CRITIC.

The shot struck the gunner beneath the cheekbone and snapped his head backward. He fell against the mount. His dead weight dragged the trigger through a short burst that stitched the stone in front of Kaze and struck the water beyond him.

Then every frightened bastard on the quay made his own decision.

—

Arthur shot the nearest guard before the man cleared his holster. His second round took the rifleman on the bridge high in the chest. The man folded over the rail, lost his grip, and dropped between the barge and the quay.

Chris ducked behind the drums as bullets tore holes through the upper row. Empty metal did little to stop them. He moved behind the stone corner instead, shoulder hard against it, ears ringing inside the mask.

“You picked the loud cover,” Teemo said.

“I’m fucking moving.”

“Right edge. He’s coming around.”

Chris let the rifle fall against its sling and drew CHOW MAIN from his right hip. The guard rounded the drums with his pistol extended. Chris shot him through the throat. The man staggered sideways, firing into the floor, and Chris put another round into his chest before he could turn the muzzle.

Blood splashed across the lowest drum. It would still be there after the ringing stopped.

Across the loading lane, a guard jabbed a Shimmer injector into his own neck.


The impact folded the guard around the gauntlet.


He didn’t get up.

A second enhanced guard came over a crate stack carrying an iron bar.

The guard tried to wrench it free.


Teeth struck the crate behind him. The man lost the bar.

His legs jerked once, then lay still. His hands scraped against the stone as he tried to rise, unable to bring the rest of his body with them.

—


The dog’s jaws closed on empty air.

Across the narrow lane, the man’s thigh collapsed between invisible teeth.

He screamed and lost the pole. The trapped leg struck a bollard; the rest of him kept moving until flesh tore and he hit the stones on his back.

The man clamped both hands over what remained above his knee, breath coming in shrill little bursts.


The pressure hit him squarely. He slammed into the shed wall, rifle flying, blood running from one ear before he slid down.

Arthur flinched at the sound from farther along the quay.

“Christ, boy.”


—

Daniel went up the loading frame.

One hand caught the crossbar. His feet found the hanging chain, toes curling around the links, and he rolled upside down beneath the bridge as a guard fired through the place his head had occupied.

“Down here,” Daniel said.

The guard looked.

Daniel’s spear lengthened through the gap between the rails and punched into him beneath the sternum. Daniel turned the shaft and pulled it clear. The man dropped his rifle and collapsed across the bridge boards, blood spreading between them.

Another guard charged from the far end.

Daniel let go.

His tail caught the nearer upright long enough to turn the fall into a swing. Bare feet struck the bridge’s side, and he came over the rail low, loose, apparently stumbling.

The guard swung his cleaver at the falling head.

Daniel’s left forearm hardened into translucent blue-white ice. He caught the wrist, pivoted under it, and drove the heel of his other hand beneath the man’s chin.

The neck broke with a sound I heard over the gunfire.

Daniel let him fall and bent to retrieve his bottle from where he’d tucked it into the frame.

Below, Chris shouted.

“Winch! They’re dropping the load!”

Daniel looked down.

The fleeing operator had pulled the release. A sling of heavy crates swung toward Chris’s corner, chain running free through the brake.

Daniel spat liquor onto the boards, annoyed at the interruption, and struck the wet bridge with his free hand.

Ice spread across the lower guide where the chain dragged through it. The links seized for an instant, shattered the first crust, then jammed against a thicker growth.

That instant was enough.

Chris rolled clear.

Kaze caught the swinging sling with his right hand.

The tendons beneath his blackened forearm thickened visibly. His fingers lengthened around the gathered cable. He stopped the load, lowered it onto the quay, then looked up at the operator.

“You throwing shit?”

The man ran.

Kaze’s left hand rose.

The operator came backward off his feet as though the air had acquired a fist around his chest. He struck Kaze’s waiting grip with his own momentum, heels scraping the stone.

Kaze drove him through the wooden side of the foreman’s table.

The money box stayed chained underneath.

The foreman looked at the wreckage, then at the thin tattooed man holding his operator by the throat.

Kaze smiled at him.

“We taking that too.”

—

The second barge began pulling away.

Its captain had cut the mooring rather than wait for anyone to untie it. Two guards crouched behind a sheet of bolted armour at the bow. One fired toward Arthur; the other tried to get a shoulder-mounted launcher above the plate.

Arthur’s revolver cracked twice. The rifleman dropped. The second man flinched behind cover with the launcher still in his hands.

“Kaze.”

“Got him.”

Black tissue crossed Kaze’s waist and hardened at his left hip. His right hand drew The Black Marrow from the living sheath, the long, black-latticed blade completing itself as he stepped through an opening onto the barge’s bow. The empty sheath sank back into him.

The guard looked up into mismatched red and purple eyes.

He tried to bring the launcher around.

Kaze cut him across the upper body. The blade passed through the weapon, through its shoulder strap, and through the man behind it. Broken metal and flesh struck the decking together.

The captain abandoned the tiller.

Kaze let the sword sink back into his hand and caught him by the back of the coat before he reached the water.

“Drive.”

The man’s boots skidded against the gunwale.

“Please—”

“Dock. Right there.”

He pointed.

The captain looked at what was left beside the bow plate and went back to the tiller.

Aye. Kaze could have moved the boat himself. He rather enjoyed having someone else discover a renewed commitment to their profession.

—

Chris reached the mechanical brake as the last shots died out.

Blood had run down his exposed upper arm from a shallow cut made by a torn edge of drum. He wiped it once, saw it wasn’t stopping him, and crouched beside the assembly.

The foreman’s surviving mechanic raised both hands.

“I didn’t shoot.”

“Then keep doing that.”

Chris examined the brake. A compact blue-lit component sat inside the housing, driving a linkage he hadn’t seen before.

A movement crossed the reflection in the brake’s polished cover.

Teemo spoke privately.

“Behind you.”

Chris turned.

A guard had crawled between the crates. He was trying to bring a knife up beneath Chris’s ribs.

Chris caught the wrist with his left hand and drove his knee into the man’s face. The knife fell. Chris shoved him backward, drew HAMMER TIME from his left hip, and fired into his chest.

The body struck the crate behind it hard enough to rock the stack.

Chris stayed over him for another breath.

Then another.

Teemo said, “He’s finished.”

“I can see that.”

“Then look at the living ones.”

Chris did.

The mechanic had sunk to his knees. Behind him, two surviving armed guards had thrown their weapons onto the stones and raised their hands.

Chris looked back at the brake.

Then at the crates.

“Billy. We’re shopping.”

His mouth opened.

The mechanic crawled backward before Billy’s first hand came through.

The change rolled outward in a wet convulsion. Chris’s small human shape folded inward around the monster emerging from it, and Catfish Billy straightened beneath the hanging chains with a low, cavernous snarl.

The surrendering guards stared up at row upon row of teeth.

One began to pray.

“Now,” Billy rumbled, “that’s a promising improvement in your manners.”

The other guard ran.

Billy caught him around the waist.

He had time for one scream before the whole head broadened, the jaw opened, and the scream went down with him.

The first guard fell to his knees.

“I surrendered.”

Billy bent close. Saliva stretched between the inner teeth.

“And so graciously.”

He swallowed him too.

The mechanic sobbed once, staring at the two empty places on the quay.

Chris’s voice came from the banjo.

“That one knows the machine. Keep him alive.”

Billy turned.

“You hear that? Employment.”

“No,” the man whispered.

Billy lifted him.

—

The mechanic landed on living flesh beside the two guards.

He scrambled backward until his shoulders struck a transparent partition. Beyond it lay another chamber he couldn’t reach. Somewhere farther off, voices echoed through passages that did not resemble any building he had entered willingly.

MEAT CANYON had three new residents.

The guard who’d tried to run shoved the other one.

“You said the dock was covered.”

“Get off me.”

“You said—”

The second man punched him in the mouth.

They hit the floor together. The mechanic dragged himself away, one hand pressed to his chest, watching them claw and strike each other in the place where all three had expected to die.

Survival had not improved their friendship.

—

Outside, Billy swallowed the disconnected brake assembly after Daniel cut it free from the frame.

That went to SHIT I NEED. The sealed crates of unfamiliar chemical stock went into DANGEROUS?, intact and away from the bell, the sign, and Charles. The money box needed Arthur’s permission before Billy approached it.

Kaze severed the chain with a thin, invisible cut. Arthur lifted the box himself.

“This stays with me.”

Billy regarded him mournfully.

“A feast laid before a starving man, and you count the spoons.”

“You just ate three people.”

“And not one had the courtesy to bring dessert.”

His cries had weakened.

Kaze looked down at them.

“He tried to stab you.”

“I know.”

“You doing all this for him?”


“I’ve already stopped him.”

Kaze’s eyes moved to the blood soaking the stones.

He shrugged and walked on.

The foreman had survived beneath the broken table. Kaze hauled him upright, took the folded route papers from his coat, and held them where the man could see.

“You go tell Silco.”

The foreman nodded too quickly.

“Tell him what?”

Kaze looked around the quay.

Then back at him.

“You need a script, nigga?”

He let go.

The foreman ran without waiting for a second invitation.

—

By the time a messenger sent back from Silco’s office reached the lower dock, the barges were still there, but the finished stock was gone.

The winch hung dead above the loading lane. Bodies lay where the fighting had left them. One injured man was still breathing beside the doorway, a rough binding around his ruined leg. The captain sat on his barge and refused to come ashore.

At Silco’s office, Jinx listened while he questioned Sevika about Vander’s rescue.

“Vi came?”

Sevika looked toward her.

“With the strangers.”

Jinx set down the spring she’d been compressing.

“You had Vander.”

Silco turned toward her.

“He was working with Grayson.”

“That wasn’t the part I asked about.”

The door opened before he could answer.

The foreman limped into the room, blood on his face and one hand clenched around the broken clasp of his coat.

Sevika stood.

“Where’s the stock?”

He looked at Silco.

“Gone.”

“How?”

The foreman tried to explain the guns, the giant, the dog, the little barefoot man on the chains.

Then the mouth.

Jinx stopped turning the spring between her fingers.

“It ate the cargo?”

“And the men.”

Silco let him finish.

“What did they say?”

The foreman wiped his mouth.

“The one with the black arm. Said to tell you.”

“Tell me what?”

The man looked helplessly around the office.

Silco understood before he could answer.

His hand closed on the edge of the desk.

“Get out.”

—

Chris came back out in the alley behind The Last Drop.

The first thing he did was check the cut on his arm. The second was look for somewhere to set the new assembly when Billy eventually released it.

Arthur carried the money box past him.

“You paying the fish man?”

“I fixed his sign.”

“Pay him rent before he discovers what you’re putting in his back room.”

Chris looked at the box.

“You got rent.”

Arthur smiled around the cigar.

“Sure do.”

Daniel came through the passage carrying his spear, a rag wrapped around the bloody head. Kaze closed the opening behind them.

Vi met them at the door.


“What happened?”

“Silco lost a dock,” Arthur said.

“And you gained a box.”

“Expensive dock.”

Kaze went past her into the bar.

Vander had managed to sit upright. He took in the group, the blood, the weapons being checked and wiped.

“Silco?”

“Wasn’t there,” Kaze said.

“You’ve made him come looking.”

Kaze’s grin showed gold above silver.

“Good.”

Vander held his gaze. Whatever thanks he owed them for the rescue, he could see the appetite standing in front of him.

“People live between you and him.”

“Then he should stop putting his shit in their houses.”

“That won’t stop them bleeding.”

Kaze’s grin faded.

“I heard you.”

He went to the table where Arthur was opening the box.

Vander watched him go.

—

Caitlyn arrived after the coin had been divided.

She came for Vander’s statement and found bloody water in a basin, a torn sleeve on the table, and Arthur counting a portion of the take into a separate pile.

“For the yard,” he said when he noticed her looking.

“Where did it come from?”

“People who were collecting.”

Her eyes moved to Kaze.

He leaned back in his chair.

“You want names? We got papers.”

“I want you to stop making more bodies while I’m still identifying the last ones.”

Arthur looked up.

“Then arrest the man paying them.”

“Give me something I can prove.”

Kaze set the foreman’s folded papers beside her hand.

“Start there.”

She opened them.

Cargo destinations. Quantities. Payment marks. Useful, though whoever had written them had been careful about names.

“Where did you get these?”

“Foreman’s coat.”

“Is he alive?”

“When I let him go.”

Caitlyn looked at the blood on the floor beneath his chair.

Then she sat down and began asking exactly what they had done.

—

Elsewhere in Zaun, the chemical-shop supplier told a colleague that two outsiders had improved a batch the proprietor had expected to throw away. Walter and Jesse had earned a roof, food, and someone else’s interest. Jesse was still insisting that the coughing worker wash before he ate.

At the freight office, Agent 47 obtained the name of a private broker and the hour when he accepted visitors. The disrupted routes had crowded too much business into too few hands. He watched the clerks long enough to learn which one everybody waited for before speaking about payment.

Far below, Singed examined the remains Sevika had sent down from the holding rooms: Deckard’s healed ear and severed neck. He made a note, then adjusted the flow to a nearby tank. Whatever grief filled the streets above him, it did not change the question beneath his hands.

And at Benzo’s shop, Ekko locked the front door himself.

He stood with the key in his palm for a moment before putting it away.

—

Silco’s office had gone quiet.

Jinx had taken her unfinished mechanism into the adjoining room. Metal clicked intermittently beyond the door. Sevika stood at the desk with a list assembled from the survivors’ accounts.

“The gunman from the cutting,” she said. “The giant. The dog. The one with the eyes. Bare feet and a tail. And the man who turns into that thing.”

Silco looked at the list.

“All of them.”

“We’ve got appearances. Some names.”

“Then buy the rest.”

“After tonight, local crews will want more than encouragement.”

Silco opened the lower drawer and took out a sealed account book.

“They’ll have it.”

Sevika watched the book touch the desk.

“How much?”

He named a sum that made her lift her eyes.

Aye. That kind of money could purchase more than killers. It could purchase patience, neighbours, a familiar face remembering which door you used.

“The dog too?”

Silco looked toward the blood the foreman had left on his carpet.

“I said all of them.”

Sevika closed her hand around the list.

Beyond the adjoining door, the clicking stopped.
