````text
The first thing Caitlyn did was stop a constable washing the blood off the step.

He stood with the bucket tilted, water trembling at the lip.

“People are walking through it.”

“Then move them back.”

He looked toward Marcus.

So did she.

Marcus stood beside the covered shape that had been Grayson. His coat was open. He had buttoned it wrong after kneeling and seemed unaware of the fact.

“Do as she says,” he muttered.

Caitlyn stepped around the bucket. She had known Grayson’s voice long enough to hear it in certain questions even before asking them. Now she had to crouch beside that voice’s silent owner and look at the broken fastener where the coat had struck the shutter frame.

She did it.

Her hands were steady until she reached for her pencil.

Inside, Ekko had found a cloth for Benzo’s face.

He laid it down, adjusted one corner, then adjusted it again. Blood kept coming through where the cloth touched the wound. Finally he stopped trying to make it look different.

Vi entered fast enough to strike her shoulder against the door.

“Where’s Vander?”

No one answered immediately.

She saw Benzo.

The force went out of her stride.

“No.”

Ekko stood.

Her eyes moved to him, to the cloth, to the wrecked counter.

“Where is he?”

The yard owner sat beside the stove with a cup in both hands. She hadn’t drunk from it. Her gaze remained fixed on the patch of floor where Vander had knelt.

“They took him.”

Vi crouched in front of her.

“Who?”

“The big one. Purple in his neck. And—”

The woman looked toward the doorway.

Marcus was visible beyond it.

Vi followed her gaze.

“And who?”

“Silco.”

Ekko turned his head.

Outside, Caitlyn heard the name too.

—

At The Last Drop, Chris and Daniel had come back from the fishmonger’s to collect Charles.

Arthur’s stolen Piltover sign stood beside him in the rear yard. Kaze set the bronze bell between the two trophies, shook the damp from his hands, and stepped back.

“All that goes inside.”

Chris hooked his fingers beneath his chin.

His jaw opened past his chest.

Something much larger gripped the opening from within. Slick flesh rolled outward, the human shape turning through itself until Catfish Billy planted his broad feet on the stones. His tail struck the empty threshold. Chris vanished inward with his gear; the enormous swamp bastard settled his hat and looked down at the pile.

I’ve watched that happen before. Familiarity has done fuck all for the experience.

Billy lifted the bell.

“A fine instrument for announcing that nobody invited you.”

He dropped it into his mouth. It rang once against a tooth before disappearing.

“Storage,” Chris’s voice snapped from the banjo. “Same with the sign. And Charles stays intact.”

Billy’s bass chuckle vibrated through his throat.

“You entrust me with your treasures, yet deny me the pleasure of criticism.”

“You can criticise him without chewing.”

The sign followed the bell. Then Billy’s whole head swelled, thick neck supporting a widening mouth crowded with rows of jagged teeth. He lifted Charles headfirst and swallowed the mechanical fish in one long, wet passage.

Inside BELLY OF THE BILLY, the three objects settled into SHIT I NEED. Chris caught the bell before it rolled against Charles’s dented head, then propped the Piltover sign beside them.

Outside, someone ran past the yard shouting for help at Benzo’s.

Arthur turned first.

Billy’s expression changed. Chris was already coming back through the opening, pulling the vast exterior inward around him. His boots hit the stones; his headlamp faced the street.

“Go,” he told Kaze. “We’re coming.”

The trophies stayed inside.

—


The dog stopped at the edge of the crowd and drew the air deep into his nose. His ears changed position.

Nobody needed to point out the blood.

Kaze entered behind him. His red right eye passed over the damage; the purple left lingered on the bodies. The faint amusement he’d carried from the cutting was gone.

Vi was already in Marcus’s face.

“You were here.”

“Stand back.”

“You were fucking here.”

He reached toward his baton.

Caitlyn caught his wrist.

“Enough.”

Vi looked at her hand, then at her face.

“Ask him.”

“I intend to.”

Marcus jerked free.

“A Shimmer brute attacked a lawful inquiry. Sheriff Grayson was killed. We have one officer who may not live through the night. You think I had time to take notes?”

Arthur leaned against the intact side of the doorway.

“Had time to keep your gun clean.”

Marcus rounded on him.

“You should be in a cell.”

“Busy day. Get in line.”

Caitlyn stepped between their sightlines.

“Did you fire?”

Marcus stared at her.

“No.”

“Why?”

“Grayson was in the way.”

She looked back at the doorway and the marks on the frame. Then she wrote his answer down.

Kaze watched the pencil move.

Vi pushed past Marcus into the shop before she did something that would prevent her leaving it. Ekko took her elbow, spoke quietly, and led her toward the rear room.

They had a frightened witness and a missing father between them. Their anger could wait only if they found somewhere to put it.


“Did he leave walking?”

She shook her head.

“Dragged. He was talking.”

“You heard him?”

“I heard him say the name.”


Kaze was already crouching beside the counter, breathing through his nose.

Blood. Shimmer. Sweat driven sharp by fear. Beneath it, the particular trace of the man who’d served them food the previous night.

He touched the smear where Vander’s coat had caught a splinter.

Then rose.

“They went out front.”


—

Vander woke to the scrape of a chair.

His hands were bound behind it. Each breath pressed against something damaged on his left side. When he tried to straighten, the room darkened around the edges.

Silco sat across from him.

There was no desk between them, only a drain in the floor and the intermittent shudder of machinery somewhere below.

“Benzo,” Vander said.

Silco rested his hands on his knees.

“You knew what involving them would mean.”

Vander lifted his head.

“Don’t put him in my mouth and call it your excuse.”

For a moment, Silco’s good eye hardened.

Then he looked toward the papers on a nearby crate.

“Names. Suppliers. Men paying twice because they can’t decide who will protect them.”

“You mean who’ll hurt them less.”

“You taught them to accept that distinction.”

Vander tested the bindings once. The movement pulled a gasp from him before he could swallow it.

Silco noticed.

Of course he noticed. Men who have loved one another can become distressingly precise about where to press.

“Tell them the collections will stop,” Silco said. “Tell them to deal with my people directly.”

“After you murdered the man they trusted?”

“After you failed to protect him.”

Vander leaned forward as far as the rope allowed.

“You’re still standing where you can talk because you’ve got somebody else holding my hands.”

Deckard shifted near the door.

The swelling behind his ear had closed, leaving a dark stain down his neck. His breathing came too fast for a man doing nothing.

Silco stood.

“There was a time you understood what independence costs.”

Vander spat blood onto the floor between them.

“You collecting that twice too?”

Silco left him with the machinery and the boy whose body had become a weapon he barely understood.

—

Two streets above the pump channels, Jesse Pinkman was trying to explain why a cracked vessel couldn’t be paid for with the promise that it had worked yesterday.

“Yesterday it didn’t have that through the side.”

The owner of the little chemical shop looked at the fracture.

“Use less heat.”

Jesse stared at him.

Walter took the vessel from his hands.

“We need something that will tolerate repeated use. This will fail.”

“Then buy another.”

Walter’s expression settled into the patient face he used when patience was becoming an accusation.

“We’re offering to repair your losses before you have them.”

Behind the counter, a young worker coughed into his sleeve. Purple residue had dried around a stoppered container beside him. Jesse watched him wipe his hand on his trousers before reaching for another bottle.

“Hey. Wash that off.”

The boy looked at the shopkeeper.

“I’m talking to you,” Jesse said. “Your hand.”

The shopkeeper frowned.

Walter set the cracked vessel down.

“Your storage is contaminating the stock. Give us a small batch of the ordinary cleaning solution. If we can’t improve its consistency, you lose nothing but an afternoon.”

“And if you can?”

“Usable equipment. Food. A place to work.”

Jesse looked at him.

Walter kept his eyes on the owner.

They’d lost the world where those two voices had made men rich and buried other men. Here, in Zaun, the first bargain was for a sound container and somewhere to sleep.

The owner considered it.

“One batch.”

Walter nodded.

Jesse waited until the man went into the back.

“You saw the kid, right?”

“I saw him.”

“That stuff isn’t just dye.”

“We don’t know what it is.”

“We know he’s breathing it.”

Walter lowered his voice.

“And working here puts us in a better position to understand it.”

Jesse looked at the vessels lined up behind him.

He’d heard variations of that sentence in much cleaner rooms.

—


The trail ran across wet timber, stopped beside a dark smear, and reappeared on the edge where a boat had rubbed its hull against the landing.

The dog thrust his nose over the water.

Kaze crouched beside him.

Something had bled there recently. Something human, already hurt. The current carried scraps, oil, wash water, and more scents than any nose could politely request.

Arthur examined a fresh scrape beneath the landing ring.

“Low boat. Heavy load.”

Vi was looking downstream.

“There are service locks. They could go under half the Lanes.”


“Some.”


Vi pointed downstream, tracing the bends with two fingers.

“Main lock there. Old pumping route underneath. The last maintenance crew blocked the western passage because the roof was going.”

Arthur crouched beside a coil of rope. A short purple fibre had caught beneath the iron ring. He left it where it was and looked at the corresponding smear on the landing.

“They stopped here to shift him.”

Vi turned sharply.

“How long?”

“Can’t tell you that.”

She looked frustrated enough to strike the ring herself.


“He was alive when they left the shop.”

“I know.”

“Then we follow what we have.”

Across the channel, a chair had scraped beneath an awning.

Kaze pointed across the channel.

“That guy does.”

A watchman had stopped winding a hoist when they reached the landing. Now he watched them from beneath a patched awning, one hand hidden behind the post.

Kaze crossed through a dark opening that appeared beside the man’s booth.

The watchman recoiled straight into his chair.

“Boat came through. Big purple dude. Man bleeding.”

“I didn’t see—”

Kaze caught his chin and turned his face.

The red pattern in his right eye held the man’s gaze.

“You did.”

His hidden hand stopped moving.

Across the water, Vi took a step forward.

“He’s talking.”

The watchman’s eyes moved as if following something inside the booth that the rest of them couldn’t see.

“Lower gate,” he said. “I opened it.”

“Where’s it go?”

“Pump stores. Old inspection dock.”

Kaze kept his hand under the chin.

“Who pays you?”

“Different men.”

“Names.”

The answer came in fragments. A foreman’s name. A description. The way the boatman had struck the gate twice with his pole. Useful little pieces, none of them a map of Silco’s soul.

When Kaze released him, the man vomited beside his chair.

Kaze pulled the hidden hand into view. A whistle lay in it.

He took the whistle.

“Get another hobby.”

He came back through the opening and dropped the little metal thing into the water.

Vi stared at his eyes.

“What did you show him?”

“Enough.”

She looked toward the lower gate.

For now, she left it there.

—

Chris found the blood still wet at Benzo’s shop.

Daniel stopped beside him with one bare foot on the threshold. His face changed when he saw the covered body. The humour went somewhere he could fetch it later.

Chris’s mask closed with its sequence of clicks and low alien chirps.

Teemo appeared in the corner of his sight: small, armoured, red lenses fixed on the ruined room.

“Watch the floor.”

“I am.”

“Then stop before you cross that.”

Chris looked down. One drag mark passed through scattered glass. His boot had nearly landed in it.

Caitlyn turned from the counter.

“Can you record what you’re seeing?”

“Did a test.”

“Will it preserve the image?”

Chris breathed out through the mask.

“Yes.”

“Then start here. Before they move anything else.”

He looked at the room, then at her.

“Arthur’s gun isn’t your problem this time.”

“It was never my only problem.”

Teemo marked the first position only after Chris asked. They worked from the doorway inward, recording the marks, the overturned counter, the broken frame. Caitlyn kept him clear of the body and wrote down where each view had been taken.

Daniel moved to the back window.

“Somebody went over this.”

She joined him.

A fresh tear in the curtain. Blood on the outer sill.

“One of the attackers?”

Daniel shook his head.

“Just somebody with blood on them. Rest would be me guessing.”

Caitlyn looked at him a little differently.

“Thank you.”

“Don’t get excited. I guess plenty.”

Outside, Marcus ordered the surviving constable moved uphill. Caitlyn went to ask where he was being taken.

Chris stayed by the counter.

Teemo’s voice turned private.

“That woman saw more than she’s saying.”

“You don’t know that.”

“She looks at the uniform before answering the question.”

Chris looked toward the stove.

The yard owner was watching Marcus through the door.

“That,” Teemo said, “is what I know.”

—

Vi led them through an inspection passage that smelled of hot iron and old water.

Arthur checked the junction behind them. Kaze moved ahead, his attention divided between the air, the floor, and the doorway at the far end.

At the gate, Vi pointed to the lock.

Kaze set two fingers against the chain.

A thin cut passed through the metal. The severed ends dropped into his palm instead of clattering onto the floor.

Vi looked at the chain, then the hand holding it.

“Could’ve used you in prison.”

“Probably would’ve left with the door.”

She almost smiled.

Almost.

Beyond the gate, a maintenance dock lay empty. Rope fibres clung to a cleat. The blood resumed at the bottom of the stairs, then continued in small drops toward a closed freight door.


“Easy.”

Kaze looked at the door.

Behind it, a chair scraped.

Vander coughed.

Vi reached for the handle.

Kaze caught her wrist before it turned.

“Move.”

She stared at him.

He pulled her sideways.

The shotgun blast came through the door where her chest had been.

Wood burst against the opposite wall. Several pellets flattened against the living black armour on Kaze’s shoulder and dropped among the splinters.

He looked at the hole.

Then smiled without warmth.

“There we go.”

The shotgun’s second barrel never fired.

Kaze put his hand through the ruined door. His forearm lengthened between the splinters, wrist turning farther than the bones of an ordinary man would permit. Fingers closed around the weapon’s action and crushed it before the gunman could pull away.

Then he pulled the man through the door.

Most of the door came with him.

The guard struck the passage floor shoulder first. Kaze followed him down, planted a knee on his chest, and tore the broken shotgun free. The man’s free hand scraped for a knife.

Kaze caught it.

“Really?”

The guard tried to wrench away.

Kaze drove the ruined weapon across his face. Bone gave beneath the metal. The second movement stopped him trying.

Blood spread between the boards under his head.

Vi stepped over him before the body had settled.

“Vander!”

Deckard came out of the room at her.


The brute hit that hand running. His own momentum folded him around it; the air left his lungs in a harsh bark.

The wall cracked.

Deckard clawed at the gauntlet. Purple veins stood out along his neck as his muscles swelled against the pressure.


Shimmer had made the boy terrifying to ordinary people. The distance between them was not something rage could cross.


Deckard spat at him and drove a knee upward.

Something in Deckard’s shoulder separated with a wet pop.

The scream carried down the passage.

Inside, Vander lifted his head.

Vi was already cutting the rope.

“Hey. Look at me.”

His swollen eye opened farther.

“You shouldn’t—”

“Finish that sentence and I’m leaving you tied up.”

He tried to laugh.

It became a cough, then a groan he couldn’t hide.

Arthur checked the second doorway with one of his heavy hand cannons raised. A guard beyond it saw the barrel and dropped behind a crate.

“Stay down there,” Arthur told him.

The man fired blind over the top.

Arthur’s shot struck the exposed hand and wrist. The pistol vanished in a burst of blood and broken fingers. The guard fell screaming behind the crate.

“Should’ve listened.”

He didn’t chase the wounded man. Another pair of boots had begun running toward them from the stairs.

The dog’s growl thickened the air.

The boots stopped.

For once, somebody in that fucking building made a sensible decision.

Kaze entered the room as Vi worked Vander’s hands free.

He looked at the injured man.

Then at Deckard, still pinned outside.

“That him?”

Vander followed his gaze.

His expression was answer enough.

Kaze stepped back into the passage.

Kaze put two fingers against the exposed side of Deckard’s neck.

A cut opened through it.

The head struck the floor beside the crushed shotgun.

Blood hit the wall, then ran down it in sheets that thinned as the pumping stopped.

No speech from Kaze. No contest.

He wiped his fingers against the dead man’s coat and went back to the room.

Vi looked at him once.

Then she put Vander’s arm over her shoulder.

—

Above them, the city’s evening trade had begun.

A man in a red mask dropped from a roof into an alley where two collectors had cornered a shop assistant. Daredevil heard the frightened breath first, then the quiet metal scrape of a blade leaving its sheath.

He landed between the blade and the boy.

The first collector swung.

A baton struck his forearm. The blade fell. Daredevil turned inside the second man’s pistol arm, drove it upward as the shot cracked between the walls, and put him against the brick hard enough to empty his lungs.

“Stay down.”

The man tried to reach the gun.

Daredevil pinned the wrist beneath his boot.

“That wasn’t a suggestion.”

The shop assistant backed away, clutching the torn front of his shirt.

“They’ll come back.”

Daredevil turned toward him.

“Who will?”

“Whoever owns them.”

He heard the truth in the terror, not a name.

When he asked again, the boy shook his head and fled.

Daredevil let him go. Beneath his boot, the collector’s heartbeat hammered against the narrow bones of the wrist.

“Then you tell me.”

—

In a rented room far from that alley, Jhin adjusted a lamp.

The man tied to the chair had been pleading until the gag made pleading useless. Now he watched the lamp shift by small degrees, each movement reflected in the polished face of the gun laid on the table.

Jhin stepped back.

His white mask caught the light unevenly. He corrected the lamp again.

“There.”

The prisoner shook his head.

Jhin regarded him with the disappointment of a craftsman confronted by material that refused to appreciate the work.

Outside, feet passed along the corridor.

He waited until they had gone.

Then he picked up Whisper.

—

At Benzo’s shop, Caitlyn closed her notebook for the first time in hours.

Marcus had supplied an account. The yard owner had supplied another. They agreed on the brute, the attack, the deaths, and Vander being taken.

They did not agree on where Marcus had been standing when Silco arrived.

She put a finger against the place where the accounts diverged.

From the doorway, Chris asked whether she needed the recording played again.

“Not yet.”

“We’re going after the others.”

“If you find Vander, I need to speak to him.”

Chris looked at the covered body behind her.

“Get in line.”

She accepted that with a small nod.

Daniel joined him outside. The street lamps were coming on, one after another, as shopkeepers decided how much darkness they could afford.

Chris glanced back once.

Teemo spoke quietly inside the mask.

“Keep the recording.”

“I was going to.”

“Somebody will want that room to have looked different.”

Behind them, Caitlyn opened her notebook again.

—

They brought Vander back through an opening into the service yard behind The Last Drop.

Vi followed close enough to keep hold of his hand.

Arthur came last with the surviving guard stumbling in front of him. The man’s ruined hand was wrapped in a strip torn from his own shirt. He held it against his chest and made a sound through his teeth every time his footing changed.

“Sit,” Arthur said.

He sat.

The opening closed.

Vander tried to turn toward the bar door.

“People—”

“Can wait,” Vi said.

“Benzo’s—”

She stopped moving.

His eyes found hers.

She shook her head once.

Vander closed his good eye.

I’ve seen strong men fight pain with every trick they know. There are kinds for which the body offers no useful defence at all.

The fish kept moving after Chris stopped watching it.

Tail. Jaw. Pause.

Above the little shop, the mechanism clicked softly through another turn. Chris stood beneath it with THE CRITIC against his shoulder and the amber lamp open on his brow. Behind that lamp lay a dead hunter’s mask, folded around a living man’s head. Inside both mask and rifle waited a soul who now remembered two lives and had been asked whether he wanted either of them precisely fucking never.

I’ve seen expensive gifts, brother. That one would keep charging interest.

Kaze came out carrying the bronze bell by its handle. Living black armour covered his right shoulder and crept across the same side of his bare chest; the rest was brown skin and dense ink. His gold upper grill caught the shop light when he opened his mouth.

Chris spoke before he could.

“If you put anybody in that bell, I’m leaving.”

Kaze looked down at it.

Then back up.

“It’s a bell.”

“You understand how little that means coming from you?”

Teemo’s voice emerged from the rifle.

“Leave the bell out of it.”

Chris’s mouth twitched. Kaze caught it, then had the sense not to reach for more.

Arthur stepped past them, hat low, cigar lit again now that nobody could complain about the filings. When a pitbull’s shoulders stand as high as a grown man’s head, that ordinary little shake has the authority of a cart losing its cargo.

Daniel came last with Charles under one arm.

The old mechanical fish was longer than the monkey-featured bastard carrying him. Daniel’s bare toes curled on the damp stones; his tail carried the bottle that would otherwise have made the arrangement impossible.

Chris pointed.

“Keep his head up.”

“He’s dead, Chris.”

“He’s a machine.”

“Then he’s taking this extremely personally.”

They turned toward The Last Drop. Hunger had survived the evening’s unpleasantness. It often does. The body has a rather cruel talent for continuing its little demands while the soul is trying to sit down.

Halfway along the street, a cart blocked their path. The driver was arguing with two men over whether the longer freight route cost him another hour or another meal. Behind the cart, a woman held a covered pot against her chest and waited for room to pass.

Arthur looked at the axle caught between the walls.

“Back it out.”

The driver turned.

Then looked at THE COUNT.

His expression changed before Arthur’s did.

“Oh,” Arthur said.

Kaze gave him a sidelong look.

“Celebrity.”

“Shut up.”

He shifted it a little sideways while the driver hauled the traces. She watched him watch it.

“That’s for my husband.”


“He’s had a bad day.”

The dog sniffed once, then let her pass.

No argument. A model citizen, provided you weren’t standing at the wrong end of his teeth.

—

Vander had put an extra table near the kitchen.

Three bowls waited there beneath an upturned tray. A strip of cloth marked one handle so the wrong portion wouldn’t go to the worker who couldn’t keep solid food down. Beside the bowls lay a list in Benzo’s thick handwriting.

The old shopkeeper was counting coins when they entered. Broad, bearded, and permanently unimpressed, he looked up at the fish in Daniel’s arms.

“You bring that through my shop, it stays outside.”

“We’re in his shop,” Daniel said, pointing at Vander.

“Practising.”

Vander took a cloth from his shoulder. He had the hands and back of a man built for breaking things, and the tired restraint of one who’d learned who usually paid afterward.

“Any more roads?” he asked Arthur.

“Only the one.”

“Keep it that way.”

Arthur pulled out a chair.

Vander put a palm on its back before he sat.

“The widow at the cutting needs someone to carry water until the pipe’s fixed. Two flights.”

Arthur stared at him.

“You taking orders for the whole city?”

“Just the bit you shot.”

Kaze laughed hard enough to ring the bell against his own knee.

Arthur’s eyes cut toward him. Then he looked back at Vander.

“Tell her morning.”

Vander released the chair.

Benzo gathered the coins into a leather purse. Beneath it, a torn piece of ledger showed columns of figures and a series of repeated marks. Vander covered the page with his hand when another customer approached the bar.

The customer wanted a drink.

Vander gave him one.

Only after the man moved away did Benzo speak again.

“She’s changed her mind.”

“About talking?”

“About talking where anyone can see her.”

Vander nodded.

“Your place. After deliveries.”

Benzo scratched his beard.

“Grayson bringing the boy?”

“Probably.”

“Then tell him to keep his bloody gloves off my stock.”

I might have smiled at that once. Benzo could make a complaint sound like a permanent feature of the earth. There was comfort in expecting him to be irritated again tomorrow.

At the table, Chris set the rifle where its optic faced the room.

Vander noticed the care he took.

“Friend settling in?”

Teemo answered.

“Still measuring the place.”

Vander’s eyes moved to the rifle.

Then to Chris.

Chris rubbed his forehead.

“Long day.”

“Food?”

“Very.”

Vander didn’t ask the next question. A decent publican knows the difference between an opening and a wound.

Vi came down from the upper room while they were eating. Pink hair, wrapped hands, shoulders that seemed permanently prepared to go through a door instead of opening it. She took one look at the fish beside Daniel and decided there were limits to the evening’s questions.

Vander handed her a bowl.

“Sit.”

“I ate.”

“When?”

She took the bowl.

Benzo snorted into his drink.

For a few minutes, the bar almost managed to be only a bar. Someone complained about the price of lamp oil. Arthur ate without contributing to the complaint.

Vi leaned against the counter near Vander.

“You going with her tomorrow?”

“Grayson? Yes.”

“Marcus will be there.”

“He generally is.”

“He looks at people down here like he’s deciding what they stole.”

Vander wiped a ring from the wood.

“Then we give him something less useful to look at.”

“You can’t keep making her stand between us and him.”

Vander’s hand stopped.

“No,” he said. “I can’t.”

Vi looked at him, hearing the admission more clearly than she’d expected.

He set the cloth aside.

“But tomorrow there’s a woman who’s afraid to tell anyone why men keep taking her money. If Grayson can help her speak, I’ll take tomorrow.”

Across the room, Kaze watched their exchange over the rim of his cup.

“You keeping that forever?” Chris asked.

“You keeping Charles?”

“Charles has potential.”

“Bell works right now.”

Daniel raised his cup.

“A devastating setback for science.”

Vi’s attention moved to them. Then back to Vander.

“Those your new peacekeeping strategy?”


“Haven’t decided what they are yet.”

“They decided?”

“I doubt they agree.”

She laughed at that despite herself.

Vander’s expression softened. He took her empty bowl when she finished, and for a moment his hand rested on her shoulder before he returned to the work.

I’ve known halls full of kings with less authority in them than that small touch. No command. No bargain. Just the reassurance that someone expected you to be there when the evening ended.

—

By morning, Sevika had the replacement freight route laid out on Silco’s desk.

She held the paper flat with a metal finger. The arm attached to that finger was no ornament; Shimmer fed the machinery that had replaced what she’d lost, and she carried its weight with the same blunt impatience she brought to most conversations.

“They can get two carts through,” she said. “Anything larger has to unload.”

Silco studied the marked street.

“Who controls the lift?”

“A man who’s discovered a passion for charging twice.”

“Temporary arrangements encourage ambition.”

“So does getting away with it.”

He looked up. The damaged side of his face barely moved; the good eye did enough for both.

“Pay him today.”

Sevika waited.

“And tomorrow?”

“Find someone who would like his position.”

A metal object dropped onto the map.

Sevika’s hand moved before it stopped rolling.

Jinx leaned over the back of Silco’s chair, blue braids dangling, eyes unnaturally bright in the lamplight. The little object wore a painted grin.

“Relax. That one’s empty.”

Sevika looked at her.

“You could try a paperweight.”

“You could try smiling. We’re both facing impossible odds.”

Silco picked up the empty casing and set it beside the inkwell.

“The upper transfer?”

Jinx’s playfulness thinned.

“Three crates. Same seals. The last one had different packing underneath.”

“Missing?”

“Not yet. Somebody’s thinking ahead.”

Sevika reached for the map.

Silco kept one finger on it.

“Verify the load before it moves.”

“I was going to.”

“Then we agree.”

Jinx drummed her fingertips against the chair. Beneath the jokes sat a weapons maker who knew when a machine had been touched, and a daughter who watched her father’s silences more closely than she watched most threats.

“What’s happening with Vander?”

Sevika went still enough for the question to acquire edges.

Silco folded the bottom of the map.

“He’s giving Piltover access to matters better settled here.”

“That sounds like him.”

“It does.”

Jinx glanced between them.

“You’re doing the voice.”

Silco turned toward her.

“What voice?”

“The one where everybody else gets half a sentence.”

He held her gaze.

“I need that shipment to arrive.”

Her jaw shifted. Then she plucked the painted casing from beside the ink.

“Fine. I’ll babysit the poison.”

She left without looking at Sevika.

The door closed. Silco let a moment pass before drawing a smaller slip of paper from beneath the map.

Benzo’s street was written on it.

—

Grayson heard the objection before Marcus had finished entering her office.

“We’re meeting criminals in another criminal’s shop.”

She continued buttoning her coat.

“We’re meeting witnesses.”

“Vander chooses them. Vander chooses where. We bring two officers because Vander doesn’t want a spectacle.”

“And you’d prefer enough men to ensure nobody speaks at all.”

Marcus set the written route on her desk.

“We should bring them up here.”

Grayson finally looked at him.

“You’ve seen what happens to people who help us and then have to go home.”

“That isn’t our doing.”

“It becomes our responsibility when we ask.”

Outside, Caitlyn stood with a folder tucked beneath her arm. Grayson took it, read the top sheet, and frowned.

“Separate from the cutting?”

“The relatives confirmed he was alive after the reported dispute. No one saw the other man return.”

“And the physician?”

“Won’t call it natural yet.”

Grayson handed it back.

“Then neither will we.”

Caitlyn glanced at the travel papers on the desk.

“I can come down.”

“Finish the witness account you started. I want the times before somebody remembers a more convenient version.”

Caitlyn nodded.

Marcus waited until Grayson moved into the corridor before collecting the route.

He folded it carefully.

That was all Caitlyn saw him do.

—

Below the freight lifts, Ekko crouched on a beam and watched the load change hands.

The Firelight beside him raised two fingers. Two armed guards on the upper platform. Another walked behind the carts, keeping his coat closed over a pistol.

Ekko looked down through his mask.

The boy Benzo still tried to feed had grown into a leader with other people depending on his decisions. His board rested under one boot. Behind his shoulder, the Z-Drive sat within reach, a small machine with an indecent claim upon the world.

A cart stopped.

One guard checked a seal.

Ekko signalled.

They dropped together.

The first guard never cleared his pistol. A Firelight struck his wrist and sent it skidding beneath the cart. Ekko landed on the rail, drove the end of his weapon into the second man’s stomach, and turned as the rear escort raised a rifle.

The muzzle flashed.

His companion jerked sideways.

Ekko caught the handle behind his shoulder and pulled.

The gunshot folded back into the barrel.

The falling body rose.

Cart wheels rolled backward over the same wet seam in the platform. The guard’s hand returned beneath his coat. Ekko stood again above them, stomach tight with a death nobody else remembered.

Three seconds.

He moved sooner.

This time his board struck the rear guard across the shoulder before the rifle cleared the sling. The shot punched through a hanging sheet of metal. His companion hit the platform alive, rolled, and came up swinging.

Ekko smashed the first crate latch.

Purple light shone between the bottles.

“Burn it.”

The Firelight pulled a charge from his belt.

A bullet struck the crate beside his hand.

“Hi!” Jinx called from the upper walkway.

Her pistol tracked them with horrible speed. Ekko kicked the charge away from the open bottles and dropped behind the cart as a second shot tore through its side.

Splinters cut his cheek beneath the mask.

“Leaving already?”

He knew that voice. His next glance confirmed the blue braids, the bright eyes, the grin that didn’t reach them.

“Back!” he shouted.

His companion hesitated over the crate.

“Now!”

Jinx’s third shot struck the board’s trailing edge as they launched. Ekko felt the shudder beneath his feet and corrected before it threw him into the rail. They cleared the platform low, taking the gap beneath the lift machinery where she couldn’t keep a clean angle.

One broken crate remained behind. Two escaped with the shipment.

Jinx looked at the bottles leaking across the boards. Then at the guard clutching his ruined shoulder.

“You lot are making this a very expensive walk.”

He tried to answer.

She was already checking the next approach.

—

Arthur carried the widow’s water four times.

On the fifth, she told him the barrel was full.

He looked into it.

Then at her.

“Could’ve said.”

“You looked like you had more in you.”

Kaze, seated on the surviving stair, bent forward laughing.

Arthur lowered the last buckets with considerable care.

“Glad you’re enjoying yourself.”

“Nigga, she got you doing community service.”

“You could carry something.”

Kaze lifted the bell an inch off the step.

Arthur stared at him for a long moment, then went down past him without a word.

He waited for the foreman’s signal before releasing its weight. Workers who’d feared him yesterday were beginning to step around his paws without asking permission.

Chris had gone back for the cold-store door. Daniel went with him, on the grounds that a man deserved an audience when fish continued ruining his life.

The city managed an hour of honest work.

Elsewhere, Marcus stepped beneath a disused stair and found Silco waiting beside the old drainage channel.

“I told you not to contact me here.”

Silco looked at the empty passage.

“You told me several things.”

“Grayson isn’t taking a payment.”

“I haven’t offered her one.”

“Then what do you expect?”

“An arrest. Vander has been protecting violent offenders. Your own reports say so.”

Marcus’s mouth tightened.

“She won’t let me take him.”

“Then let her see what her protection has purchased.”

Silco held out a purse. Marcus didn’t reach for it.

“No trouble at the shop.”

“You’ll have your opportunity to leave with a prisoner.”

“That isn’t what I said.”

Silco’s hand remained extended.

The water beneath them carried a thin purple sheen.

Eventually Marcus took the purse.

—

Benzo had cleared his counter for the ledger.

He’d also put his best tools away before Marcus could find a reason to handle them. A petty precaution, and one I wish had been the only necessary sort.

The yard owner stood near the rear curtain, wringing her gloves. Vander stayed beside her. Grayson listened while she explained the second collection, then asked which mark belonged to which payment.

“That one’s the usual.”

“To whom?”

The woman glanced at Marcus.

Grayson turned her head.

“Wait outside.”

“Sheriff—”

“Marcus.”

He left.

Benzo watched the door close.

“Could improve every room that way.”

Grayson ignored him with the ease of long practice.

“The other mark?”

“They changed it last month,” the woman said. “Different men. Same day.”

Vander leaned over the paper.

“Who told you not to mention it?”

The first crash came from outside.

Not a shot. Wood breaking under a body.

Grayson had her pistol out before the yard owner finished flinching.

“Behind the counter.”

Benzo reached beneath it instead.

Vander moved toward the door.

Another impact shook the shutters. Through the glass, a blue sleeve crossed the window at the wrong height and vanished.

Then someone screamed.

Grayson stepped into the doorway with her pistol level.

Deckard hit her from the blind side.

He had once been a thin street thug desperate to look harder than he was. Shimmer had made the lie flesh. Purple veins climbed his throat; one shoulder stood grotesquely higher than the other. His forearm struck Grayson across the chest and drove her into the iron edge of the shutter frame.

The sound stopped Benzo in his tracks.

Her gun fired into the stones. She sagged against the frame, trying to draw breath through a chest that no longer moved properly.

Vander lunged.

Deckard caught him by the coat and slammed him backward into the counter. Glass burst around his shoulders. The yard owner crawled behind the stove, both hands over her mouth.

Benzo came out with the heavy shop wrench.

“You little bastard.”

He struck Deckard behind the ear.

The blow would have dropped an ordinary man. Deckard staggered, then turned with blood running into his collar.

Benzo raised the wrench again.

Deckard caught his wrist.

Bone broke beneath the grip. The wrench fell. Before Benzo could pull away, Deckard drove his other hand into his throat and hurled him against the projecting corner of a dismantled press.

I’ll spare you nothing that matters: his head struck first. The press did not move. Blood ran down the iron in a narrow sheet while his legs folded beneath him.

Vander roared and hit Deckard hard enough to turn his face.

He hit him again.

On the third swing, Deckard buried a fist beneath his ribs. Vander’s breath came out wet. The brute drove him to his knees, one hand locked in the back of his coat.

Marcus stood outside with his pistol in his hand.

Grayson lay a few feet from his boots.

He looked from her to the doorway and could not seem to make the two sights belong to the same afternoon.

Silco stepped into view behind him.

“This wasn’t—” Marcus began.

Silco glanced at the pistol.

“Put that away.”

Inside, Vander lifted his head.

Blood covered his lower lip.

“Silco.”

There are names a man says as though he’s found an old wound open beneath his clothes.

Silco looked past him at Benzo.

Then at the ledger.

“You were always very particular about who was allowed to hurt this city.”

Vander tried to stand. Deckard forced him back down.

Behind the stove, the yard owner pressed her face into her gloves.

Silco picked up the ledger pages.

“Take him.”

Marcus made a small, broken sound.

Silco turned.

“You have wounded officers to attend to.”

The surviving constable groaned near the broken cart outside. Marcus looked toward him, then back at Grayson.

Her eyes were open.

He knelt.

“Sheriff?”

No answer.

“Grayson.”

He pressed his hand against her neck, shifting it as though a better position might change what he found.

Behind him, Deckard dragged Vander out through the shop. His heels left two tracks through the glass.

—

Ekko returned by the roofs because his board was pulling left.

He landed above Benzo’s street, annoyed at the damage, still carrying the recoil of that vanished gunshot in his stomach.

Then he saw the gathering crowd.

The broken shutter.

The blue coat on the ground.

He dropped the last distance without the board.

Someone tried to catch his arm.

He tore free.

“Benzo?”

Inside the shop, the counter stood crooked. Tools lay under glittering glass. A woman made a thin, continuous sound behind the stove.

Ekko saw the boots first.

Then the body.

His hand flew to the Z-Drive.

Stopped.

Outside, somebody said the attackers had gone several minutes before the whistle brought help.

Several minutes.

Ekko stood with his fingers around the handle. Three seconds ago he had been in the doorway. Four seconds ago he had been crossing the street.

He could take those steps again.

Benzo would still be lying there.

The boy lowered his hand.

I’ve no clever thing to say about that, brother.

He knelt beside the man who’d always asked whether he’d eaten.

And for a long while, he could not make himself touch him.

KAZE VS. MULTIVERSE — CHAT CORRECTIONS / PROJECT UPDATE HANDOFF
Collected through October 4, 2026. WORK MODE. NO PLAYBACK. DO NOT RESTART.

PURPOSE AND AUTHORITY

Do not make him a generic rescuer, a passive spectator, a paperwork investigator or only an irritated quip machine. His diagnoses do not automatically cause his villainy.

## Personality / social behavior

Daniel is friendly, easily sidetracked, quick-witted, absurdly funny and heavily dad-joke prone. His verbal thinking is sharp: he follows a conversation and remembers his sentences. Apparent losing-the-thread or forgetting is deliberate deception when he chooses it, not a default slow-minded gag. He can laugh at his own line or deliver a terrible pun seriously. Actual unconsciousness/blackout keeps its separately established limits.

His Wukong-like mischief is biological, behavioral and martial: hanging upside down while talking, climbing inconvenient structures, appearing at an unexpected angle, playful baiting, physical competitions and reciprocal one-upmanship. **Daniel is drunk twenty-four seven because he constantly drinks hard liquor.** No sober combat mode; he is not merely imitating intoxication. **External movement:** Drunken Master + breakdance + lucha-libre rotations.

Daniel carries a substantial **large-ish clear glass bottle of hard liquor**, without VODKA text or branding. **Wukong-like magic replenishes the liquid; Cryomancy controls temperature.** These are separate from container strength. Ongoing replenishment supports his perpetual drinking; pouring/spitting for approved combat remains physical. The initial vessel is **breakable**. If broken/lost, any replacement/enchantment requires actual acquisition/access rather than a bottle silently respawning. Refill does not duplicate a stolen bottle, guarantee return, grant invulnerability, or sober Daniel.

Daniel progresses by **observation → attempted imitation → adaptation → practice → permanent integration of compatible principles**. Byakugan supplies information; mythic simian imitation/improvisation supplies an aptitude; Saiyan training supplies real physical development; none is an arbitrary stolen power source.

First imitation can be fast yet incomplete, mistimed, overpowered, inefficient or unsuccessful. No compulsory mistake quota; a compatible simple principle may click promptly. Actual repeated use or meaningful application establishes mastery. **DRUNKEN SYNTHESIS** is the process of making a lesson work with Daniel's own drunken movement, limbs, weapons, energy and Cryomancy rather than cosmetically copying another fighter. **PROOF** denotes a genuine integrated mastery/breakthrough, not alcohol quantity, XP or a count of acquired moves.

He learns from opponents, friends, mentors or legitimate observations. He cannot copy a soul, species, memories, artifact, divine office or absent energy source by watching. hard_negatives:
- id: KAZE_NO_COMBAT_CLAWING
  value: false
  meaning: No claw swipes, scratches/rakes, or claw-hand fighting substitute.
- id: FLESHLIGHT_MATTER_TRANSFER
  value: false
  meaning: Hat-aperture observation does not pass hands, weapons, objects, salvage or ammunition.
- id: FLESHLIGHT_AUDIO_CAPTURE
  value: false
  meaning: The local FLESHLIGHT live video, replay and saved clips contain images only; no new exterior microphone,
    audio track or inbound-audio route.
- id: FLESHLIGHT_REPLAY_WORLD_CONTROL
  value: false
  meaning: Local pause/replay controls do not pause, rewind, restore or control exterior events, Billy, swallowing
    or digestion.
- id: FLESHLIGHT_RECOIL_SUPPORT
  value: false
  meaning: THE FLESHLIGHT cannot brace THE CRITIC or route recoil.
- id: FLESHLIGHT_OUTSIDER_VIEW_IN
  value: false
  meaning: Outsiders cannot look through Billy hat aperture into BELLY OF THE BILLY.
- id: BANJO_MATTER_TRANSFER
  value: false
  meaning: Banjo is outward audio, not a matter channel.
  value: false
timed bark may serve roast-relay response.
- id: BLACKLIGHT_SOUL_DISGUISE
  value: false
  meaning: Biological disguise does not copy unique soul/divine/conceptual identity or authority.
- id: PROJECT_PRESENTATION_OWNS_CAUSALITY
  value: false
  meaning: Presentation follows resolution and cannot choose outcomes.
- id: COUNT_HIGH_NOON_SIMULTANEOUS_DUPLICATES
  value: false
  meaning: HIGH NOON and THE COUNT are two states of one transforming primary platform, not independent simultaneous
    primaries.
- id: COUNT_ALLSPARK_CONSCIOUSNESS
  value: false
  meaning: AllSpark contribution supplies machine-life reflex/adaptive coordination only; THE COUNT and Arthur cybernetics
    do not gain an independent mind.
- id: TEEMO_CRITIC_JARVIS_AI
  value: false
  meaning: Current Teemo-in-THE-CRITIC is Teemo soul-consciousness bound to the rifle, not AI/JARVIS/aimbot/omniscient
    computer.
- id: CATFISH_CURRENT_SELF_ESCAPE_PRELOAD
  value: false
  meaning: Billy-controlled release/regurgitation is the only currently established BELLY OF THE BILLY exit; future
    Penitentiary breakout mechanism stays unresolved until earned.
- id: ARTHUR_PREBLAST_CYBER_PRELOAD
  value: false
  meaning: Historical pre-blast scenes still cannot preload Cyber-Arthur. At the current Second Temporal Relaunch
    pilot opening, Cyber-Arthur, UNSHAKEN, HIGH NOON/THE COUNT and AllSpark/IDC Power Stone integration are carried
    earned state.
- id: KAZE_NARUTO_OCULAR_PACKAGE
  value: false
  meaning: Old Kamui/Kokugan remains retired; s29 right Eternal Mangekyō/left Six-Tomoe replacement is current. Images
    cannot override it.
- id: MINI_BILLY_STABLE_COEXISTENCE
  value: false
  meaning: No mini-Billy exists in current execution; inside-out switching preserves one exterior body and the inactive
    full-size partner inside.
- id: CHRIS_BILLY_EXTERIOR_STATE_INERTIA
  value: false
  meaning: Chris or Billy being the current exterior state does not itself justify keeping that state; the owner resolves
    switching from actual motive, utility, timing and agency with no quota.
- id: RAPID_BOND_SWITCH_INVULNERABILITY
  value: false
  meaning: The rapid bond switch is near-instant but grants no teleportation, phasing, invulnerability frames, automatic
    restraint escape, injury reset or position reset.
- id: UNCLE_RUCKUS_ACTIVE_NARRATOR
  value: false
  meaning: Uncle Ruckus is removed from active narration. Black Mimir is sole narrator.
- id: PRESENTATION_CHANGES_RESOLVED_CAUSALITY
  value: false
  meaning: Presentation CRFA may change disclosure and style only; it cannot rewrite resolved events, chronology,
    actor choice, mechanics, injuries, deaths, resources, knowledge or consequence.
- id: OFFSCREEN_MEANS_PAUSED
  value: false
  meaning: Materially active actors/factions continue from their own motives off-camera; tiered simulation is a performance
    strategy, not a pause.
- id: BIG_NAME_SURVIVAL_OR_DURATION_PROTECTION
  value: false
  meaning: Fame, franchise importance, roster status, protagonist/villain role and future usefulness never grant extra
    reactions, exchanges, phases, speeches, durability or survival.
- id: NARRATOR_STORY_STRUCTURE_AWARENESS
  value: false
  meaning: Black Mimir may derail emotionally but never narrates episode/plot/story construction as in-world fact.
- id: SWALLOWED_EXPLOSIVE_PROPAGATION
  value: false
  meaning: Explosions after legitimate Billy intake do not injure Billy or BELLY OF THE BILLY occupants; this does
    not universalize to exotic nonphysical effects.
- id: PENITENTIARY_FUTURE_SEASON_FORESHADOW
  value: false
  meaning: CATFISH PENITENTIARY may grow visibly in Season Two, but narration never advertises a future-season payoff.
- id: KAZE_BASELINE_VISIBLE_BLACK_MARROW
  value: false
  meaning: Black Marrow is not visibly carried at baseline; Kaze manifests it from/reintegrates it into his body.
- id: OMEGA_TEEMO_PRELOAD_BEFORE_MASK_TEST
  value: false
  meaning: Current Teemo stays post-ASU and Critic-only until the future on-screen first completed Predator-mask test
    triggers the Omega transition.
- id: PREDATOR_MASK_FULL_SUITE_PRETEST
  value: false
  meaning: Mask is not yet transferred/integrated at reboot root; full suite requires actual engineering/testing.
- id: ARTHUR_CHRIS_LINK_REMOTE_CONTROL
  value: false
  meaning: Cross-dimensional link shares information/calls only; it never grants remote body, weapon, aim or Dead
    Eye control.
source_layers:
  PROJECT: hot execution runtime and controlling active owners
  NOTION: control plane / staged and committed decisions / source map / relations; not mutable-state authority
  GOOGLE_DRIVE: deep archive / originals / large files / backups / old cutovers / cold evidence
  GITHUB: versioning / diffs / rollback / validator and compiler scripts / automated tests
  READWISE: optional external research intake/highlights; never canon by storage alone
  status: Architectural roles only. No external service is required or certified installed; all controlling owners
    are in the clean manifest. Optional archives/tools never outrank those owners.

# KAZE ANIME — WORLD & MECHANICS ACTIVE CORE

## GEN-II s22 AUTHORITATIVE PILOT / COMBAT / PRESENTATION REINFORCEMENT

This overlay is a scoped correction over s21/s20/s19. It does not create CRE-15+, alter the accepted checkpoint, or authorize unrelated redesign.

### No-name-protection / no-duration-protection hard lock

Canonical definition: **Universal causal combat resolution — no name protection** below. Apply the S27 causal-latency section for exact timing. This redirect adds no separate exception, reaction window or duration floor.

### Kaze impatience / pattern interruption enforcement
Kaze's established impatience, pattern recognition, Stasis Tolerance, Closure Predator, Conscious Bait Acceptance and related psychology must materially affect causality. Once legitimate evidence lets him recognize stalling, repeated tactics, obvious behavioral motifs, manipulative routines, transformation/ritual setup, fake suspense, redundant explanation or a delaying pattern, do not preserve the planned sequence merely so another actor can finish it. Kaze may interrupt, attack, reposition, break the setup, force the point, call it out, deliberately play along, accept bait because he wants the confrontation, or leave. Pattern recognition remains inference and can be wrong; it grants no unsupported motive, hidden mechanic, future event or production knowledge.

### Off-screen causal centers as scenes
Whole-world advancement remains mandatory. Montage/summary is a compression tool, not a replacement for all independent lives. When an established off-camera actor/faction produces a materially meaningful discovery, decision, conflict, relationship change or new independent thread, Presentation CRFA should consider a real scene before compressing it into montage. No new individualized NPC is invented merely to satisfy this rule.

### S22 pilot presentation boundary

The controlling Act I spine is event/objectives.yaml#/act_I. Human Vander operates The Last Drop. Bandle retaliation remains a later causal lane, never a competing immediate cold-open destination. No Avengers/Endgame, Dragon Ball or Naruto recap.

## GEN-II s20 AUTHORITATIVE EXECUTION / NARRATIVE-INTEGRATION OVERLAY

This overlay supersedes lower conflicting presentation, protagonist-gravity, passive-progression, team-combat or playback-audit language. CRE-00 through CRE-14 remain the only shared simulation engine; no CRE-15+ is created.

### Autonomous off-screen life / no protagonist gravity
Advance materially active actors and factions from their own motives, obligations, relationships, resources, geography and information whether or not the main group is present. They may travel, work, rest, heal, train, investigate, bargain, fight, fail, change relationships, gain/lose resources, become injured or die without Kaze involvement. Entire conflicts may begin and end without the main group.

Do not turn “off-screen life” into nonstop plot. Ordinary living, recovery, maintenance, travel, downtime and unresolved waiting are valid when supported. Use **simulation tiers** for efficiency: fully resolve causally hot centers; advance background centers at the minimum fidelity needed to preserve real state until pressure makes them materially active. Tiering never pauses them, erases consequences or fabricates unseen achievements.

### Conflict-origin diversity
Conflict must arise from actual incompatible goals, territory, resources, evidence, retaliation, politics, protection, ideology, deception, social pressure, environment, pursuit, siege, traps, accidents or chain reactions. Do not default to “Kaze sees someone and wants to fight.” First meetings may remain nonviolent; allies may become enemies later; enemies may cooperate temporarily; conflicts may outlive the scene that created them.

### No-convenience sidelining / progression participation
Earned progression must change what a character can reasonably choose to do. Do not keep a capable developed character passive, absent, trapped, parked in BELLY OF THE BILLY or otherwise conveniently uninvolved merely because another character is easier to write. Participation is still decided by that character's actual motives, injuries, knowledge, responsibilities, positioning and choice; this rule is not a screen-time quota or forced-combat command.

Cyber-Arthur is therefore field-active by default when Arthur would reasonably participate. BELLY OF THE BILLY is transport/shelter/workspace/containment, not Arthur's automatic combat parking spot.

### Cooperative combat / team synergy
Allies and enemies may fight as teams rather than adjacent isolated 1v1s: cover, setup attacks, create openings, rescue/reposition, restrain, flank, crossfire, combine compatible abilities, exploit learned habits and adapt communication. Coordination quality comes from actual familiarity, trust, communication, compatible capabilities and experience. New/uneasy allies may interfere with each other. Teamwork can improve effectiveness but never adds power levels together, guarantees success or erases a decisive mechanical mismatch.

### Pre-playback QA gate

Canonical gate: `canon/presentation/PRESENTATION.md` → **PRE-PLAYBACK QA GATE**. One silent material-source pass, including S27 structural-function repetition and causal latency; fix locally before release. No duplicate audit loop.

### Presentation CRFA / resolution firewall
After causal resolution and consequence completeness, route presentation through the dedicated Presentation CRFA before Black Mimir render. Narrative architecture may change **disclosure**, not reality. Story-time and discourse-time remain separate; nonlinear presentation never pauses or advances the current world clock by the duration of a flashback. Objective flash-forwards cannot invent unplayed future canon.

Derived genre profiles, repetition trackers, theme notes, camera salience and other presentation metadata are disposable views, not canon or actor knowledge.

### Structural variety / no formula
Canonical structural decision: **S28 sequence-level repetition decisions**. Presentation CRFA varies disclosure of resolved facts. Independently valid unresolved proposals may differ, but novelty never changes a resolved objective, setting, choice or outcome. Causal repetition, meaningful rhyme/contrast and plain direct presentation remain legal.

### Major-event visibility
Off-camera events may be learned through aftermath, report, flashback or later discovery. A newly irreversible milestone must become clearly legible to the audience when its omission would make accepted state unintelligible, unless explicit authority moved it off-screen. This does not force every death or fight to be shown live.

### Execution priority
When style and substance conflict, resolve in this order: **causality → character/source fidelity → clarity → emotional consequence → style**. Cool presentation never repairs or overrides a bad causal result; fix causality first.


## GEN-II s19 AUTHORITATIVE EXECUTION OVERLAY

This overlay supersedes any lower section that still describes a fixed 16-part event, a fixed ten-minute delivery target, an older narrator voice, an automatic narrator rotation, a pre-s18 capability gate, or a pre-s19 first-relaunch checkpoint. CRE-00 through CRE-14 remain the only shared simulation engine. Detailed character mechanics remain in their owning logical modules; this engine owns shared execution/validation procedure.

### Capability-routed functional abstraction — project-wide
For every consequential candidate, resolve **problem -> project domain -> relevant actor/system function -> current-state availability -> canonical mechanic owner -> mechanically valid combination -> resistance/interference -> actor choice -> consequence**. Functional categories are retrieval folders, never powers, move menus, quotas, or permission to skip owner detail. New earned mechanics normally attach to an existing function; create a new top-level function only when the problem class is genuinely distinct. Capability is always separate from present availability. Unknown stays unknown.

### World-first steady state
Advance every materially active causal center through the same legitimate elapsed interval before camera choice. Off-camera means unshown, never paused. Preserve actor intent, faction ecology, evidence carriers, custody, resources, injuries/forms, relationships, institutions and environmental consequences. Camera then selects pressure/salience with zero incumbency, no forced rotation and no main-character teleportation. Fixed imported and fixed Runeterra participants carry a season-level meaningful-POV obligation only while they remain causally available. Accepted death, destruction, permanent removal or blocking may terminate that obligation **before any POV occurs**; roster coverage never delays a fight, prevents death or grants survival. Main group remains approximately 55–70% of Season-Two presentation overall, not per part.

### Universal causal combat resolution — no name protection
Every fight, duel, ambush, pursuit clash and multi-party combat resolves from the participants' **current** source-faithful capabilities, speed, reactions, durability, resistances, skill, knowledge, psychology, injuries, forms, equipment, resources, terrain, positioning, intent, interference and actual choices. Fame, franchise importance, protagonist/villain status, roster status, audience expectation, future usefulness and planned screen time provide **zero** survival or duration protection. Anti-plot-armor is equally forbidden: a famous or important character is not killed merely to prove stakes when the mechanics do not support it.

When the whole matchup is decisively one-sided and the advantaged actor legitimately recognizes enough of that fact to act on it, resolve the encounter at the speed their actual intent and methods imply. Do not manufacture trading sequences, transformation ladders, monologues, comeback phases, repeated ineffective attacks, arbitrary restraint, forgotten abilities, delayed finishing blows or inflated durability to make a big-name fight feel longer. Unknown mechanics may legitimately change the matchup when revealed; immediately reassess from the new evidence rather than granting either side a scripted phase.

Kaze receives no special narrative protection and no competence suppression. His full currently earned toolkit, self-sovereign psychology, pursuit behavior, lethality, adaptation, overkill and actual information state resolve normally. If he genuinely chooses to kill and possesses a legitimate immediate route, the target survives only through real mechanics, resistance, escape, interruption, changed Kaze intent or another causally supported route—not because the target is important later.

### Hard futures / no survival armor / no choreography forcing
Committed future objectives constrain authorial preference only while real causality leaves compatible outcomes available. They **never** authorize miracle survival, competence suppression, automatic failure, delayed lethal action, durability inflation, teleportation, knowledge, access, forced stupidity or any other intervention that changes a mechanically and psychologically supported result merely to preserve a later beat. If legitimate actor choice plus mechanics permanently kills, destroys, removes or otherwise forecloses a participant needed by an older future objective, record the consequence and retire/reclassify the incompatible objective unless an already-established resurrection, return or equivalent mechanism actually preserves it. Irreversible milestones remain on-screen unless newest explicit authority specifically moves that progression off-screen.

### Presentation ownership

Canonical owner: `canon/presentation/PRESENTATION.md` → **EPISODE IDENTITY**, **FIRST-PRESENTATION / NEW-VIEWER ORIENTATION** and Black Mimir voice/POV sections. Continuing a current provisional episode does not require a newly recovered header or repeated first discoveries. No second narrator or actor knowledge is created.

### Delivery

PRESENTATION#act-delivery-contract exclusively controls three-episode Acts, PLAY/NEXT and 25–30 minute Spruce targets. Plan one whole Act prospectively before Episode 1; no filler or forced causality. The prospective remaining VII–XII / optional XIII Arcane spine is in objectives; old eight-Act and earlier ceilings do not control.

Latest Kaze Q&A locks are owned by the Main Seven Canon for morality/brutality/project-specific combat and by the Psychological Bible for internal psychology. This master validates the mechanics underneath them and prevents dramatic examples from becoming accidental new systems.

- A behavioral preference for catastrophic overkill does not guarantee a result against every target. Repeated rebounds/collisions do not create infinite energy, automatic exponential multiplication, or guaranteed damage.
